title: Clean Claim Performance System: Start Here Guide (Version 1.1, September 2026)
summary: Seven-page orientation to a ten-file bundle. Describes three linked control layers (front-end clearance, authorization tracking, denial root-cause control), a five-phase 30-day start-up, two recorded handoffs and a weekly/weekly/monthly review rhythm built on one owner, one next action and one due date per case. No numbers, definitions or payer rules; misdescribes its own workbooks.
top_ideas: Every open exception gets exactly one owner, one next action and one due date; anything missing one of the three is treated as unmanaged.
Trace each preventable denial to the upstream step that caused it and place a prevention control there instead of only reworking the claim.
Record handoffs between work lists as they happen using a shared key, so a denial can be traced to its origin without relying on memory.
Separate a short weekly forward-looking exception review from a monthly root-cause review, and recheck each control against a recorded baseline.
red_flags: Promises automatic calculation, but the front-end kit's status column has no formula, so the weekly huddle's urgent and watch counts stay at zero.
Tells users to record the queue ID on the authorization tracker; the tracker has no such column, so the 'connected loop' is free-text only.
No statistics, definitions or payer rules; 'at-risk' and 'authorization-sensitive' are never defined, and neither named KPI is calculated in any kit.
Assumes an appointment-based office with seven staff roles; script-generated and released weeks after first build, with no evidence of field use.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Front-End Control Kit: Pre-Service Clearance Queue and Weekly Huddle (Excel workbook, v1.1, September 2026)
summary: Nine-sheet Excel workbook for pre-service clearance: a 200-row queue, eligibility, registration-audit, referral, financial-clearance and escalation logs, a weekly huddle sheet and a 30-day recheck. Mostly empty tables with dropdowns. The status column that should flag urgent cases has no formula, so the huddle counts stay at zero. Nothing is Medicare- or facility-specific.
top_ideas: Log every eligibility check as evidence: workflow stage, date, source, result, subscriber mismatch, other-coverage concern and follow-up owner.
Audit a weekly sample of registration data against source documents, categorise defects and treat results as process improvement, not discipline.
Carry denial-feedback fields on the upstream issue record: caused a denial, category, dollars, root cause confirmed, prevention control updated.
Track process-compliance measures (share of open cases with owner and due date) beside lagging outcome measures.
red_flags: 'Suggested Clearance Status' column has no formula in any of 200 rows; the huddle's urgent and watch counts therefore always read zero.
'Active' count includes closed rows and 'open escalations' misses three awaiting statuses; dropdowns accept any typed text without an error.
All twelve recheck measures are typed by hand and undefined; nothing links the six logs to each other or to the other kits.
Built for scheduled office appointments and patient estimates; no Medicare Advantage, hospice, secondary-payer, dual-eligibility or facility fields.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Prior Authorization Control Kit: Tracker, Expiration Watchlist and Payer Change Log (Excel workbook, v1.1, September 2026)
summary: Eight-sheet Excel workbook: a 200-row authorization tracker with a calculated risk flag, a manual expiration watchlist, an empty payer requirement matrix, a payer change log, a denial and appeal log with deadline urgency, a weekly review sheet and a 30-day recheck. Formulas work but never clear finished cases, inflating urgent and watch counts. Contains no payer rules.
top_ideas: Payer rules matrix where every entry carries its policy source, the date the source was last checked and an owner.
Payer change log that closes a notice only when workflow, reference matrix, staff communication and a verification check are all done.
Before billing, confirm an authorization or referral matches the delivered service, dates, rendering provider and location.
Flag appeal and peer-to-peer deadlines by days remaining, with a closed state so finished cases stop flagging.
red_flags: Risk formula tests closure last: served approved cases turn WATCH after expiry and past-dated denied cases stay URGENT, inflating weekly counts indefinitely.
Appeal urgency has no closed state: upheld and closed cases stay URGENT, reversed ones stay WATCH; the count 'fixed' in v1.1 inherits this.
Tracker has no patient/account or queue ID column; watchlist is a blank copy-paste table; calendar days used where business days are stated.
No payer content and no mention of 2026 federal decision deadlines; original Medicare visits need no authorization, so most of it sits unused here.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Denial Control Kit: Monthly Dashboard and Root-Cause Meeting Pack (Excel workbook, v1.1, September 2026)
summary: Excel workbook for a monthly denial review: monthly totals and seven category amounts feed a denial rate, recovery rate, category shares and a dollar rank; supporting sheets cover pattern logging, a root cause register, payer pattern review, actions, a 30-day recheck and a timed agenda capped at three decisions. One month only, undefined inputs, no code mapping or targets.
top_ideas: Specify each corrective control as failure statement, containment, durable control, trigger, workflow location, stop rule, audit method and success measure.
Rank denial categories by dollars monthly and commit to at most three decisions, each with one owner, due date and evidence of completion.
At recheck, ask whether a category fell from better workflow, changed volume or re-categorisation, and whether another category rose instead.
When a category is concentrated in one payer, open a payer file: stated reason, policy source, suspected change, contact, containment, escalation date.
red_flags: Recovery rate excludes unresolved denied dollars and reads near 100% when write-offs are not posted; not comparable with the playbook's 75% benchmark.
Denial rate and denied dollars are undefined (denial versus rejection, charges versus expected payment); blank inputs display as 0% and $0.
Neither headline KPI is calculated: payer denial rate is an optional typed cell and clean claim rate is absent; the dashboard keeps one month only.
Seven categories do not match the companion playbook's five; no remittance-code mapping; ties in dollars blank a row of the top-three agenda table.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Clean Claim Performance System: Release Notes (Version 1.1, September 2026)
summary: Four-page release note for version 1.1, the first public release. Lists the ten files, the changes made after an internal build weeks earlier, a version-numbering rule, a no-updates purchase policy and three scope limitations (no integration, payer variability, limited support). Discloses no testing or defects and miscounts its own playbooks.
top_ideas: Keep a dated version log for every procedure, agent instruction set and reporting workbook, written before the change goes live.
Publish a known-limitations note with each internal tool or dashboard, including real defects, data sources and what is not checked.
Disclose calculation fixes by naming the measure and how its definition changed, and restate history when a definition changes.
Write down the advice boundary: what a tool or agent may decide and what must go to a qualified person.
red_flags: Purchase excludes all future updates, and five of the ten files are sold separately; the bundle's unique content is 11 pages and three workbooks.
Calls its limitations 'not defects' while shipping a front-end workbook whose status column has no formula; no defect list or test record is given.
The v1.1 fixes were patched in by script and never re-saved in Excel; the 'fixed' urgent appeal count still includes upheld and closed cases.
Internal errors: says four playbooks were replaced when the bundle has three, and labels the wrong table row as 'This document'.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Federal IDR Playbook - No Surprises Act Independent Dispute Resolution: How to Challenge a Payer's Out-of-Network Payment - and Win
summary: Vendor guide to using the No Surprises Act federal arbitration process against commercial out-of-network underpayments: eligibility, deadlines, QPA, statutory factors, offer strategy, an expected-value filing test, batching, a dispute log and 90-day rollout. Procedural timeline is mostly right, but benchmark advice conflicts with statute and scope exclusions are missing. Near-zero fit for a Medicare-based facility practice.
top_ideas: Before pursuing any dispute or appeal, run an expected-value test: win-probability-weighted recovery minus fees and labor; pursue only when positive, using the practice's own win rates.
Keep a dispute log with fixed status codes that computes each next legal deadline at entry and treats any missed deadline as a zero-tolerance metric.
Triage every non-contracted remittance within five business days to decide which dispute regime applies and whether the payment falls below the payer's own stated benchmark.
Write short dispute briefs: aim for the more credible number, not the largest; three arguments, five pages, led by encounter-specific facts; review every loss to improve templates.
red_flags: Tells readers to anchor offers on the Medicare fee schedule and FAIR Health charge percentiles; the statute bars arbitrators from considering public-payer rates and usual-and-customary charges.

Never states that Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, TRICARE and VA claims are outside the process; batching example implies Medicare Advantage claims are eligible; ERISA/state-law rule is garbled.
Core numbers rest on unverified post-June-2026 events: $15 fee, June 11, 2026 batching rule, August 11, 2026 en banc ruling; no citations; portal address looks wrong.
ROI math inconsistent: 85% win with 20% loss; $300 both 'file' and 'not worth filing'; batch costs still use old $115 fee; batching omits 30-business-day service window and cooling-off.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: HIPAA Privacy and Security for Revenue Cycle Playbook
summary: Guide to HIPAA duties inside billing: vendor agreements, role-based access, patient access to billing records, breach assessment, Security Rule controls and vendor oversight, delivered as a six-domain audit, recurring calendar and 90-day plan. Core framework is sound but uncited, has several rule errors, offers no templates, and ignores AI agents, state law and facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Keep a register of every vendor that touches patient data, with agreement status and content checks, reviewed yearly and at each onboarding or renewal; extend it to AI vendors.
Give every user and software agent its own identity with role-scoped access; ban shared logins and review access logs quarterly.
Log every misdirected statement, claim or email as an incident and document a four-factor breach assessment started within a day.
Run a compliance calendar with one named owner: annual risk analysis, agreement audit and training; quarterly log reviews; event-triggered tasks for new vendors, systems and incidents.
red_flags: Calls January 25, 2013 the Omnibus effective date (it was publication) and declares all pre-2013 agreements non-compliant; content, not signature date, is the test.
Says access fees cannot be flat (HHS allows a flat fee for electronic copies) and attributes an annual risk-analysis mandate to current guidance; that is only proposed.
Zero CFR citations, no named author, unsourced enforcement counts, and a penalty table labelled 'Corrected Figures'; rulemaking status and dollar amounts need checking against primary sources.
Tells practices a vendor's breach notice starts their clock, ignoring the agency rule; silent on AI vendors, Florida's 30-day breach law, family-member disclosures and Change Healthcare.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Medicare ABN Compliance Playbook: The Form Nobody Completes Correctly - and the Revenue Nobody Recovers
summary: Vendor guide to the Medicare ABN (CMS-R-131): mandatory versus voluntary notices, field-by-field completion, delivery rules, GA/GX/GY/GZ modifiers, a denial-based exposure audit, a five-stage workflow, a 90-day plan and two checklists. The workflow skeleton is usable, but core rules on voluntary notices, Field C, Field E, course-of-treatment notices and appeals contradict CMS instructions.
top_ideas: Build a service-level trigger list from the practice's own Medicare denial history, mapped to NCD/LCD indications and frequency limits, and check it before the service.
Reconcile medical-necessity and frequency denials to a notice log every month, classify each as coding error or true coverage gap, and feed results back into the trigger list.
Gate every patient-liability notice on payer type: CMS-R-131 only for Original Medicare; Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and duals need their own process.
Encode GA/GX/GY/GZ as a claim-edit rule tied to documented notice status, and keep one owner for form-version control against the CMS website.
red_flags: Says statutorily excluded services cannot be billed to the patient without a voluntary ABN; CMS treats that notice as a courtesy with no effect on liability.
Tells staff to put the MBI in Field C and tick reason boxes in Field E; CMS bars Medicare numbers on the form and Field E is free text.
Calls denials without an ABN final and non-appealable, and bans course-of-treatment notices; denials are appealable and CMS allows one ABN for repetitive care up to a year.
Contradicts itself on modifier GY versus GX, on timing, and on routine notices; no author, citations or links; form-revision dates (March and May 2026) unverified.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: No Surprises Act Compliance Playbook: What Your Practice Must Do, What It Must Not Miss, and What Is Still Coming
summary: Vendor playbook on the No Surprises Act good-faith-estimate duty for uninsured and self-pay patients: who triggers it, business-day deadlines, content, notices, the $400 dispute process, penalties, a ten-step workflow, template, 90-day plan and checklists. Core mechanics mostly right; content list, co-provider enforcement and penalty math are unreliable. Almost inapplicable to a federal-program, facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Gate the rule by coverage category first: federal-program patients fall outside it, so only truly uninsured or commercially insured patients paying cash enter the estimate workflow.
Start the estimate from the scheduling event with business-day deadlines and keep proof of delivery date and method, instead of handing it over at check-in.
Compare every self-pay bill with its estimate before release; hold anything $400 or more above it until the reason is documented or the bill is reduced.
Use the free CMS model notice on the website and wherever cost questions arise, and run a small monthly sample audit of estimates for existence, content and timeliness.
red_flags: List of 'required' GFE elements departs from 45 CFR 149.610(c)(1): invents an expiration-date element, drops mandated disclaimers; the template inherits the gaps yet claims full compliance.

Penalty section multiplies every self-pay visit by $10,000 to show $1.8M-$9.6M yearly exposure; no enforcement action cited, state-first enforcement ignored, and a CMS self-disclosure route appears invented.
Treats co-provider charge itemization as an enforced failure point; omits HHS enforcement discretion, the 12-month recurring-service rule, and provider duties during a patient dispute.
Says 'no exemptions' while its own table exempts federal-program patients; cites an August 2026 en banc Fifth Circuit ruling and other dated status claims with no citations.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Awareness Playbook
summary: Plain-language primer on the physician self-referral law and Anti-Kickback Statute for independent practices. Method: inventory every financial arrangement with referral sources, screen with a short checklist, send flagged items to healthcare counsel, repeat annually. Sound triage routine, but no regulatory citations, several wrong or outdated technical rules, and little that fits a facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Keep a living register of every financial arrangement with referral sources and screen each on four points: written, fair market value, matches services actually delivered, no link to referral volume.
Draw the line at action: staff may inventory and flag, but structuring, changing, ending or disclosing any arrangement goes to independent healthcare counsel first, never the hospital's lawyers.
Screen everyone against the OIG exclusion list and SAM before engagement and monthly, keep a log, and track gifts and meals per physician against the annual non-monetary limit.
Tie medical-director pay to documented duties and hours at fair market value, and treat turnkey vendor service lines with volume-based fees as kickback risks needing review before signing.
red_flags: Outdated overpayment rule: teaches the 'should have identified through reasonable diligence' trigger that CMS replaced on January 1, 2025 with a knowledge standard and a 180-day investigation pause.
In-office ancillary rules misstated: patient notice applies only to MRI, CT and PET, not therapy or radiation; solo physicians qualify without a two-physician group; turnkey billing logic is wrong.
Says per-click equipment rent from referring physicians can comply and that recruitment money cannot pass through the joining practice; regulations bar the first and expressly allow the second.

No regulation citations or Stark and kickback penalty amounts; FY2024 figures self-contradict (558 called second-highest against a 543 record); silent on facility directorships, copay waivers, EKRA, Florida statutes.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: The KPI Action Guide for Independent Practice, Volume I: The Core 10
summary: Vendor guide applying one five-step routine (threshold table, root-cause segmentation, ranked interventions, floor execution, durability test) to ten standard revenue-cycle KPIs. Conventional, mostly sound operating advice built for staffed office practices; benchmarks are unsourced, some codes are wrong or invented, and nothing addresses Medicare, Medicare Advantage or facility-based billing specifics.
top_ideas: Give every KPI both a benchmark and a separate act-now threshold, then segment by payer, provider, reason code, age and dollars before choosing any fix.
Daily exception queues: denials touched within 48 hours, follow-up ranked by dollars within age bucket, and no claim left without an action taken and a next follow-up date.
Write-off governance: monthly reason-code trend, dollar-tier approval matrix, tracing every timely-filing loss to its origin, and a quarterly look-back for recoverable balances.

Daily missing-charge report plus monthly encounter-to-charge reconciliation, with hospital and facility encounters tracked separately; count an improvement as real only after 90 days of normal operations.
red_flags: Reason-code guidance is unreliable: PR-27 is mislabeled (prior-to-coverage is CARC 26), CO-4 is filed under registration, and the 'ANSI error codes 004/005/021' match no standard X12 list.
Every benchmark is unsourced; body text still carries correction notes from earlier drafts, and the HFMA 2-4% cost-to-collect figure is a hospital-style number applied to small practices.

Chapters contradict each other: 45-50% patient collection called strong while net collection must exceed 95% and bad debt stay under 1% of charges; cost-to-collect ranges and per-claim costs disagree.

Medicare Advantage escalation advice is off: MA and self-funded plan disputes generally sit outside state insurance commissioners, and CMS coverage-criteria (2024) and prior-authorization (2026) rules are ignored.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: The KPI Action Guide — Complete Bundle, Volume II: Specialty & Situational KPIs (Chapters 11–15)
summary: Volume II covers five situational KPIs (prior authorization approval, coding accuracy and E/M distribution, credentialing lag, referral conversion, bad debt) through a repeated five-step scaffold. Process advice is sensible but prose-only, with no templates. Benchmarks are unsourced, every table has a defect, and Medicare-specific rules that matter to a facility-based practice are missing.
top_ideas: Compare each clinician's E/M level mix with public CMS specialty data quarterly, audit outliers, and separate documentation shortfalls from code-selection habits; rebuild around facility visit code families.
Start enrollment and credentialing the day an offer is accepted, log weekly status contacts per payer, and build a revenue-at-risk model for every new hire.
Segment every rate by payer, provider or source before acting, and call a fix durable only after two consecutive periods inside target.
Keep hardship write-offs and true bad debt under separate adjustment codes, measure adjudication-to-first-statement days, and trace a sample of write-offs backward each quarter.
red_flags: Editor-facing revision notes left in three benchmark tables, plus misfiled cells; the 82, 90% approval band is pinned on unnamed KFF '2025' reporting that looks misattributed.
Names locum tenens and billing under a supervising physician's NPI as credentialing-gap options without Medicare's limits; omits the filing-date effective-date rule and 30-day look-back.
Self-contradictions: Medicare enrollment '120 days not unusual' versus 30, 45 days; typical commercial timeline flagged as failure; bad debt targets on net revenue and gross charges cannot both hold.

Ignores rules in force in 2026: federal prior-authorization decision deadlines (72 hours, 7 days), dual-eligible billing ban, Medicare copay-waiver limits, and overpayment refund duty after coding audits.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: The Universal Specialty Billing Framework: A Complete Foundation for Specialty Revenue Cycle Intelligence
summary: Foundation volume for the vendor's specialty guides. Argues specialty billing needs payer-specific intelligence: an eight-question payer map, monthly payment-variance checks, a four-dimension code risk rating, a prior authorization program, 48-hour documentation feedback and step lists for three denial types. Prose only, surgical examples, one sourced statistic, several rule errors, no templates or targets.
top_ideas: Keep a living per-payer file (contract terms, real denial and payment behavior, policy changes, named contacts) and review it quarterly with the physician-owner.
Check every month that allowed amounts match contracted rates by payer and code, and escalate persistent gaps through the contract's dispute process.
Rate the practice's main codes for audit, overlap and modifier risk, then aim documentation checks and audits at the codes that score worst.
Give each clinician encounter-specific documentation feedback within 48 hours, and log every denial by payer, service and reason so appeals follow evidence.
red_flags: Says Medicare Advantage plans may use criteria that differ from LCDs; rules effective January 2024 (42 CFR 422.101, 422.138) restrict that. No mention of the 2026 prior authorization timeframes.
Modifier errors: AS listed as covering CRNAs (it covers PA, NP, CNS); modifier 25 appeals said to need an unrelated problem, which CPT and NCCI do not require.
Unsourced or inflated numbers: $3,000-$12,000 weekly physician time loss, 3% variance trigger, and the claim that three denial types make up most denial volume.

Built for surgical specialties; nothing on facility E/M, care management, eligibility or timely-filing denials. State insurance commissioner escalation generally cannot reach Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, VA or Tricare.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Behavioral Health
summary: Applies the vendor's billing framework to outpatient behavioral health: payer mix, time-based psychotherapy coding, authorization and concurrent review, documentation failures, parity-based appeals, telehealth, and five revenue opportunities, ending in five operating standards. Useful structure, but unsourced, with material errors on collaborative care billing, E/M leveling with psychotherapy add-ons, authorization prevalence and payment figures.
top_ideas: Per-payer fact sheet answering fixed questions: authorization triggers, where criteria are published, telehealth rules, rates for top codes, filing limits, enrollment requirements, regulatory history.
Note templates that force the billing-critical element (minutes, scored measure, necessity statement) at the point of documentation for every time-based service.
Look-ahead calendar putting every expiring approval in front of billing two weeks before it lapses.
Behavioral health integration and collaborative care as a monthly care-management line billed from the treating-practitioner side, after verifying rules the document gets wrong.
red_flags: Says collaborative care codes 99492-99494 pay the psychiatric consultant; Medicare has the treating practitioner bill them. Requirements omitted; revenue estimate unreliable.
Allows E/M leveling by total time alongside a psychotherapy add-on, contrary to CPT, and pushes sessions toward 90837 using an unsourced 60%/20% code-mix threshold.

Claims most commercial payers and TRICARE require authorization for routine outpatient mental health; current guidance says otherwise. Parity strategy ignores that Medicare and Medicare Advantage are outside the statute.
No citations anywhere; dollar figures overstated (group therapy at 50-60% of individual rates, testing at $150-$300 per hour at Medicare rates); '80% of practices' statistic unsourced.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Cardiology
summary: Applies the vendor's framework to cardiology: Medicare-heavy payer mix, professional versus technical billing, code tables for diagnostics, catheterization and devices, four authorization tiers, documentation and denial patterns, five revenue opportunities and five look-back audits. Operational ideas are sound, but roughly a third of code-table rows and most dollar figures are wrong or outdated; no sources cited.
top_ideas: Transitional care capture: discharge feed, documented contact within two business days, visit within 7 or 14 days, bill the transitional care code instead of an ordinary visit.
Registry with a period-end billing trigger for any service paid per period; direct fit for monthly chronic care management and annual wellness eligibility.
One maintained billing map tying each service to code, modifier, place of service and supervision rule, plus audits for claims paid at the wrong amount.
Advance care planning capture audit: document content, participants and minutes for every goals-of-care conversation and bill 99497/99498.
red_flags: Remote monitoring coding is wrong: 93297/93298 are 30-day codes, 93299 was deleted in 2020, ICD remote is 93295; payment figures conflict between sections.
Code tables unreliable: catheterization, TEE, stress echo, generator-change and interrogation descriptors are wrong; PCI branch add-on codes 92921/92929 were deleted January 1, 2026.
States non-ischemic cardiomyopathy has no ICD waiting period; NCD 20.4 applies the same exclusions plus three months of medical therapy. Shared decision-making requirement omitted.

Dollar figures overstated two- to three-fold (nuclear technical component $800-$1,200, cardiac rehabilitation $35-$50 per session); physical-presence supervision rule outdated since January 2026; no citations.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: ENT (Otolaryngology) - Two Complete Revenue Cycles, One Independent Practice
summary: Specialty overlay arguing ENT practices manage surgical billing carefully but under-bill office procedures. Covers payer behaviour, CPT tables, modifiers, five authorization categories, documentation failures, denial patterns and revenue opportunities, ending in five operating standards and look-back audits. Control ideas are sound; many code descriptors, the sinus-surgery global period and the dollar figures are wrong or unsourced.
top_ideas: Treat each service line as its own revenue cycle with its own documentation standard, charge trigger and audit.
Expiry calendar with a 45-day renewal alert and no claim released without a live authorization.
Payer-by-code rule table (modifiers, units, coverage quirks) maintained by billing and updated whenever a denial shows a rule changed.
Appeal only when the record meets the payer's written criteria and itemize the supporting entries; otherwise fix documentation prospectively.
red_flags: Tells readers to add modifier 50 to 31231 and bill it with 31235; the code already covers both sides and is bundled into same-family endoscopies.
Puts sinus surgery in a 90-day global needing modifier 58 or 79 for debridement; Medicare assigns those codes a 0-day global. Modifier 25 is never mentioned.
Wrong descriptors for 31255, 31267, 42415, 69631, 69641, 69660, 92602 and 95165; omits the 2018 sinus combination codes and multiple-endoscopy reductions.
Unsourced dollar figures ($115 endoscopy, $400-$600 balloon, $718,000 a year) and advice to merely correct billing going forward when codes lack note support, ignoring refund duties.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Geriatrics
summary: Office-centric geriatric billing add-on arguing revenue sits in CCM, TCM, AWV, cognitive assessment and E/M leveling, with Medicare Advantage run plan by plan. Useful program skeletons; no templates, sources or fee-schedule year. Several code rules are retired, outdated or wrong, and one recommended code combination is prohibited. Reviewer spot checks used secondary sources; cms.gov was unreachable from this session.
top_ideas: Bill monthly care-management codes from a time log with a month-end trigger and automated conflict checks, separate from encounter-based charge capture.
Quarterly audit of place of service and code family against the patient's actual setting for providers working across facilities.
Per-plan Medicare Advantage operating sheet plus annual contract review against Medicare rates for the practice's own top codes.
Discharge tracker with clocks for the two-business-day contact and 7/14-day visit, limited to discharges to community settings.
red_flags: Recommends billing 99483 with 99497 and 99215 on one date as 'not upcoding'; CMS guidance bars 99483 with same-day office E/M and advance care planning.
Says an ABN applies when an MA plan may not cover a service (ABNs are Original Medicare only) and that MA plans need not follow Medicare rules.
Lists retired or non-payable codes as live with rates: G0505 (replaced 2018), 99339/99340 (deleted 2023, wrongly described), 99358 (not recognised by Medicare since 2023).

Outdated rules (CCM/TCM same-month ban, written CCM consent, TCM medication-reconciliation deadline) and unsourced statistics; revenue estimates are gross, ignore staffing cost and contradict each other across sections.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Neurology
summary: Specialty overlay claiming neurology is underbilled, not underpaid. Covers payer mix, EEG, EMG and drug code tables, botulinum toxin units, authorization categories, documentation failures, denials, and opportunities in visit levels, care management, transitional care, sleep and telehealth. Process controls are reasonable, but EEG descriptors, EMG logic, several drug codes, the 99215 criteria and the headline arithmetic are wrong.
top_ideas: Structured report headers capture the facts that set the code (duration, state, count, time); coders select only from those fields.
Code-concentration screen (one code above 80% of a category) to detect default coding, followed by a small sample audit in both directions.
Pre-claim reconciliation of billed units against documented units for anything billed by unit or time.
Care-management registry with consent, care plan and monthly time log, reported as its own revenue line; discharge-notification workflow for transitional care.
red_flags: EEG table inverted: 95816 and 95819 are routine codes, 95812 and 95813 extended; 95830 and 95836 are not ambulatory EEG; 95827 was deleted in 2020.
The 99215 criteria given are the moderate tier, so following them upcodes 99214 visits; the $520,000 example ignores its own 40% premise (about $208,000).
Wrong drug codes (J3030, J3031, J1020-J1030, A9588, unclassified codes for lecanemab); no discarded-drug JW/JZ rule for botulinum toxin; stand-alone EMG codes paired with nerve conduction codes.
Encourages a billed visit on every infusion day; care-management and transitional-care sections omit one-biller limits, consent, risk and community-discharge conditions; no sources anywhere.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: OB/Gyn
summary: Vendor specialty add-on arguing OB/Gyn is three revenue cycles (maternity global, office gynecology, surgery) needing separate written workflows. Useful operating habits (counters, payer reference sheets, pre-bill edit checks, look-back audits) sit on unreliable technical content: misused antepartum codes, mislabeled CPT/HCPCS codes, wrong Medicare statements, uncited revenue figures. Nearly irrelevant to a facility-based geriatrics practice.
top_ideas: Give each distinct billing environment its own written, payer-specific workflow and refresh the payer reference sheet at every contract renewal.
Attach a counter to any bundled or frequency-limited service so reaching the threshold automatically raises a billing review.
For a preventive visit that also handles a problem, bill the problem work with modifier 25 and warn the patient about cost-sharing at scheduling.
Open each improvement with a 90-day look-back audit to size the leak, rebill what is recoverable and justify a permanent control.
red_flags: Headline advice to bill 59425/59426 for visits beyond 13 on top of the global is wrong; those are antepartum-only codes. Following it creates duplicate, unbundled claims.
Code errors: 58572 called 250 g or less with BSO (actually over 250 g); G0101 and Q0091 descriptions swapped; N80.0/N80.1 are non-billable headers; newborn care placed inside the global.
States Medicare patients are by definition over 65, that Medicare covers no obstetric care, and that it covers an annual well-woman exam. All three are wrong.

Uncited dollar figures and payer rules that look invented: payers credentialing surgeons by robotic approach, most payers requiring authorization for version, accreditation needed for ultrasound technical billing, $60,000-$100,000 ultrasound upside.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Oncology
summary: Vendor specialty add-on for independent medical oncology: drug-claim precision plus professional billing accuracy, with code tables, authorization categories, denial patterns and five standards. Sound process ideas, but wrong drug units and codes, a wrong complex CCM time threshold, blanket 99215 advice and missing JZ/sequestration rules. Only its CCM, navigation, ACP and visit-level passages touch geriatrics, and those need verification.
top_ideas: Sweep the full active census monthly for care-management code eligibility, with care plan and time log, using verified CMS thresholds and consent rules.
Reconcile every claim to the source clinical record before submission and require a documented sign-off.
Hold a fixed question set per payer covering every reimbursement component, not just professional fee rates, and refresh it when services change.
Make any clinical change that alters payer requirements automatically notify billing or authorization before the next service.
red_flags: Says complex CCM (99487) is billable at 20 minutes of staff time; CMS requires 60 minutes plus moderate or high complexity decision making. Billing on that threshold is an overpayment.

Drug table errors: bevacizumab J9035 per mg (actually per 10 mg, a tenfold overbilling risk); liposomal doxorubicin on deleted J9001; Q5117 called subcutaneous trastuzumab; discontinued J9070 still listed.

Urges 99215 at nearly every infusion visit citing prescription drug management and lab review, which support moderate complexity; never mentions modifier 25. Blanket upcoding advice with audit exposure.
Outdated or missing: JZ modifier, sequestration on ASP plus 6, consent and coinsurance for CCM and navigation; 96423 and 99601 misdescribed; EOM cancer count wrong; ESA rule misstates MDS.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Orthopedics
summary: Orthopedic overlay to the vendor's universal billing framework, framing revenue loss as a precision problem. Covers payer environments, surgical code risks, implants, prior authorization, documentation failures, denial patterns and five revenue opportunities. No usable tools or sources, and several coding statements (ultrasound guidance with 20611, meniscectomy plus chondroplasty, multiple-procedure percentages) conflict with CPT, NCCI or Medicare rules.
top_ideas: Run each payer class (Medicare, each Medicare Advantage plan, Medicaid, others) as its own workflow with a separate rule sheet, KPIs and review cadence.
Capture evidence payers later demand at the first encounter through templates, then answer payer criteria point by point with record pointers in authorizations and appeals.
Quarterly audit of payer-applied payment reductions against contract and Medicare rules, disputing errors in writing; underpayments never surface as denials.
Benchmark each provider's E/M distribution against published data with encounter-specific feedback, and keep a standing audit-readiness protocol with a named response team.
red_flags: Tells practices to bill 76942 with 20610, 20611 or 27096 and audit for 'missed' guidance codes; 20611 and 27096 already include guidance, so this is unbundling.
Calls meniscectomy plus chondroplasty separately reportable and gives multiple-procedure reduction as 100/50/25; CPT bundles chondroplasty into 29880/29881 and Medicare pays 100/50/50.
Spine 'professional fees' of $15,000-$40,000 repeated three times with no source; Medicare surgeon payment for a lumbar fusion is a few thousand dollars.
E/M advice pushes 99205 using exam detail (irrelevant since 2021) and an unworkable '15 points below benchmark at 99215' test; no sources, tools, author or date.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Pediatrics
summary: Pediatric overlay arguing billing habits, not Medicaid rates, cap revenue. Covers preventive visits with modifier 25, vaccine administration, screening codes, telephone and after-hours billing, Medicaid plan authorizations, eligibility denials and pediatric chronic care management, with worked revenue arithmetic and five standards. Specific but unsourced, with material errors on 90472, modifier 33, audio-only codes and VFC billing.
top_ideas: Per-plan reference sheet for every managed-care payer (authorization list, timely filing, resubmission and appeal steps, carve-outs), owned by billing and updated on each provider bulletin.
Verify eligibility at every encounter, with a second check on the service date and an escalation path for coverage gaps.
Hard-wire charge capture: required template fields trigger the code, and a monthly report compares codes billed with services documented.
Claim look-back method: sample 30-90 days for one service line, compare notes with codes, price and annualize the gap, fix the system rule, refile within timely filing.
red_flags: Standard 2 and Section 7 count 90472 units per vaccine component; 90471-90474 are per vaccine administered, so this overbills every non-counseled combination vaccine.

Calls modifier 33 an after-hours modifier (it is the preventive-services modifier) and prices established-patient calls with new-patient audio-only codes 98008-98010, which Medicare does not recognize.
Revenue totals ($265,200, $187,200, $75,000) apply full commercial rates in a Medicaid-heavy specialty and ignore VFC per-vaccine fee caps and payer cuts to same-day E/M.
Says VFC product-code billing is always a compliance violation and audit recoupment covers every encounter; both are overgeneralized, state- and payer-dependent rules.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Primary Care & Family Medicine
summary: Office-centric primary care billing essay: level visits by decision-making, bill preventive plus problem visits, and build care-management, transitional-care, wellness and advance-care-planning workflows, backed by quarterly audits. No sources or templates; ignores facility visit codes, G2211 and APCM; misstates transitional-care service date, medication-management leveling, advance-care-planning frequency and incident-to supervision.
top_ideas: Hard pre-bill gate on monthly care-management claims: consent, current care plan, time threshold and designated billing practitioner verified, otherwise hold the claim.
Benchmark each clinician's visit-level distribution against public Medicare utilization data for the same code family; review outliers quarterly in both directions.
Discharge-triggered transitional-care sequence: alert within 24 hours, contact within two business days, visit inside the 7- or 14-day window.
Quarterly internal coding audit of a fixed sample per clinician (top visit levels, modifier 25, care management), plus payer performance reported by plan and product.
red_flags: Says prescription drug management makes a visit moderate complexity 'by definition', supporting 99214, contradicting the two-of-three rule it states; following it would upcode.
Instructs billing transitional care with the discharge date as service date; CMS uses the face-to-face visit date. Omits decision-making level and community-discharge requirements.
Advance care planning framed as first 30 minutes 'in a calendar year' needing five minutes of documentation; no 16-minute minimum. Incident-to physical-presence rule outdated; setting limits ignored.

No citations, dated rates or templates; revenue figures assume 100% uptake and ignore labor; contradictory statistics; nothing on G2211, APCM, complex CCM, facility visit codes or split/shared visits.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Radiology & Laboratory
summary: Fifty-page add-on to the vendor's billing framework arguing imaging and lab revenue is lost through underpayment and unbilled work. Covers payer behavior, code tables, the professional/technical modifier matrix, imaging authorization, lab coverage and ABNs, documentation gaps, denial patterns, five opportunities and five standards. Useful operating habits, but uncited and wrong on several codes and Medicare rules.
top_ideas: Audit paid claims for underpayment and down-coding as a control separate from denial work; short-paid claims never appear in denial reports.
Reconcile what the record shows was done against what was billed on a 30-day sample, then create charges automatically from the documentation event.
Check coverage rules at ordering and again before the claim leaves, using a short reference of covered indications for the highest-volume services.
Run a small quarterly claim-to-source audit whose findings change templates and billing rules, then sweep correctable claims inside timely filing.
red_flags: Treats the ABN as usable for Medicare Advantage patients; it is an Original Medicare form. Also mislabels national lab coverage policies as contractor LCDs.
Code errors: 78816 and 76817 descriptors wrong; lung lobe and colon cancer resections taught as Level V pathology (they are Level VI); Z82.49 mislabeled.
Outdated or self-contradicting: HbA1c screening has been covered since 2024; appropriate-use text says consultation is required, then a note says the rule was rescinded.
Headline $910,000 MRI example rests on a $350 Medicare technical rate that looks far too high; the 15-25% unbilled-test statistic has no source.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Specialty Companion Guide: Rheumatology
summary: Forty-page add-on arguing rheumatology practices over-rely on infused biologics. Covers payer steering, biosimilars, drug and injection code tables, ultrasound guidance, visit leveling, biologic authorization evidence, denial patterns, five opportunities and five standards. The authorization and documentation advice is reasonable; the drug table, ultrasound billing, infusion-visit and care-management claims contain material errors and no citations.
top_ideas: Make payer criteria required structured fields in the visit note so authorization and audit evidence is created at the visit, with a no-criteria, no-submission gate.
Keep a product-to-billing-code reference, verify every drug claim against it, and audit drug dispensed against code billed each quarter.
Track payer formulary and policy notices, list affected patients immediately, and follow a fixed ladder: exception request, peer-to-peer, documented transition.
Treat the largest service line as a concentration risk, and run care management from a registry that starts with the highest-complexity patients.
red_flags: Ultrasound guidance advice invites unbundling: 76942 cannot be billed with 20604, 20606 or 20611, and the real Medicare gain is about $35, not $60-$100.
Drug table errors: rituximab J9312 and belimumab J0490 are per 10 mg; J1020-J1040 were deleted in April 2024; intravenous ustekinumab is J3358, not J3357.
Tells practices to add an office visit to about 80% of infusions with no mention of modifier 25 or the separately-identifiable requirement: an audit trap.
Says every inflammatory arthritis patient qualifies for CCM because cardiovascular risk is 'universal', ignoring consent, time and one-biller rules; site-of-care description is backwards.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: KPI 01: Denial Rate by Payer
summary: Playbook for running denial management off payer-level denial rate: rate bands, three cause families, reason-code and trend diagnosis, eight interventions, a two-week rollout, backlog triage, escalation and a weekly dashboard. Sound operating discipline, but no formula, no sources, one wrong CARC meaning (252), missing eligibility codes, and nothing on Medicare, Medicare Advantage or appeal deadlines.
top_ideas: Manage denials per payer (and per Medicare Advantage plan), never as one blended rate; one plan can be in crisis while the average looks fine.
Diagnose with a 90-day reason-code frequency table per payer, a 12-month trend to separate step changes from drift, and a by-provider split.
Change one thing at a time, then gate claims before submission against that payer's top three denial reasons.
Call a fix durable only after three months under threshold, a changed reason-code mix and reproducibility from the written procedure; keep a weekly payer grid and annual audit.
red_flags: CARC 252 is defined as 'referring/ordering provider not found'; the X12 meaning is that an attachment or other documentation is required to adjudicate.
No formula for denial rate, no group codes, no appeal or timely-filing deadlines, no payer-specific rules; every statistic is unsourced.
Threshold contradictions: per-payer crisis line is 15% in the table but 12% in the text; 'action threshold' is 8-12% in one section and 12% in another.
Front-end branch treats CARC 96/167/272 as eligibility failures and omits the real eligibility, wrong-payer, hospice and bundling codes (22, 24, 27, 109, B9, 236).
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: KPI 02: Clean Claim Rate
summary: Playbook treating clean claim rate as a front-end quality score: bands, two measurement points, four quality dimensions, rejection-reason ranking, eight preventive interventions, phased rollout, monthly and quarterly audits, near-miss tracking. Useful configuration controls, but no formula or real rejection codes, confused rejection/denial boundaries, false absolutes, and heavy front-desk assumptions that do not fit facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Track acceptance at two points, clearinghouse and payer front end, under one written definition, and keep both separate from post-adjudication denials.
Rank rejection reasons over 60 days, cut by payer, claim type and user, and trace five rejected claims back to source when reports are unclear.
Run configuration controls: quarterly NPI and enrollment audit against NPPES and payer records, per-payer claim-template audit with locked defaults, payer-specific scrubber rules kept current.
Sustain with a monthly top-three rejection comparison, a quarterly 25-claim trace per payer, and a count of near-misses caught before submission.
red_flags: No formula; blends scrubber pass rate, acceptance rate and first-pass payment, so its bands cannot be compared with outside benchmarks.
Calls a 95% clean claim rate with an 8% denial rate 'in conflict', then says rejections and denials are different events; files authorization failures as rejections.
False absolutes: scrubber setup is done 'once' with 'immediate and permanent' gains, and a low rate is 'always' the practice's fault.
Advises an open-ended hold on resubmitting rejected claims with no warning that the timely-filing clock keeps running; lists 'rejection codes' without one real code.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: KPI Prescription Series, KPI 03: Days in AR
summary: Generic primer on days in AR: definition, five threshold bands, a five-report diagnostic sequence (payer-level, aging, charge lag, denial age, patient AR), eight matched interventions, a 90-day recovery plan and a monitoring cadence. Sound framework; unsourced numbers, several wrong payer-timing statements, two arithmetic errors, no worked calculation or templates.
top_ideas: Compute days in AR per payer and against the same month last year; a blended number dominated by fast Medicare payments hides a deteriorating plan.
Manage leading inputs (charge lag by provider and service type, first-pass acceptance, age of unworked denials) because the headline number lags by one to three months.
Same-day denial categorization by cause, dollars and nearest deadline, plus a named owner and a defined substantive first action within a set number of days.
Fix the upstream cause first, then run a time-boxed recovery project that ends with a forced write-off-or-pursue decision on whatever remains.
red_flags: Charge-lag script turns a one-time $10,800 float into '$43,200 a year' by an unexplained multiplication; the promised 5-8 day improvement is two to three times its own inputs.
Payer-speed statements are wrong or misleading: Medicare's 14 days is a payment floor, not a ceiling, and 60-plus-day Medicaid or 45-day MA payment conflicts with federal prompt-pay standards.

Says AR older than 90-120 days from service is typically uncollectable and expired-appeal denials should be written off; ignores Medicare's one-year filing limit, 120-day appeal clock and reopening rights.
No sources, no worked calculation, formula left unspecified (charge window, gross versus net, credits); claims a 5% rate premium can lose to faster payment, which fails in steady state.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: KPI Prescription Series, KPI 04: AR Aging Buckets
summary: Guide to managing the AR aging report by shape: target shares for five buckets, three diagnostic cuts (insurance versus patient, payer-level, worked versus unworked), bucket-matched interventions, a Monday review, age-based work queues, a write-off projection and a new-provider test. More operational than KPI 03 but unsourced, with deadline and transaction errors and no Medicare specifics.
top_ideas: Track each aging bucket's share weekly and treat two consecutive weeks of growth, or any growth past 120 days, as the trigger for diagnosis.
Measure the worked share of aged claims and audit a sample of claim histories to separate payer slowness from follow-up failure.
Queue by age band with deadline proximity overriding dollar value, and force a documented pursue-or-write-off decision on every item older than 120 days.
Project next quarter's write-offs from the oldest bucket using the practice's own measured recovery rate, giving a forward-looking reserve for cash planning and sale diligence.
red_flags: Appeal deadline stated as 90-180 days from service date; appeal clocks normally run from the denial date, and Medicare, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid rules are never mentioned.
Says claim receipt can be batch-checked via ERA; an 835 exists only after adjudication, so lost or rejected claims go unnoticed. Acknowledgement and status transactions are the right tools.
New-provider test is impossible as written (61-plus day claims within a provider's first 60 days); write-off cross-check compares dollars with a rate; 30-50% recovery figure is unsourced.

Patient-collection and write-off advice omits Medicare cost-sharing rules (QMB billing ban, hardship or reasonable-effort standard) and blends insurance claims into a collections-agency referral after insisting they be separated.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: KPI 05: Point-of-Service Collection Rate
summary: Vendor guide to point-of-service collection rate: the share of known, collectible patient responsibility collected before the patient leaves. Method is front-desk behavior change backed by pre-visit benefit verification, scripted payment requests, payment plans, a prior-balance policy, staff scorecards and onboarding. Office-based, commercial-payer assumptions; no sources, formula or full scripts. Almost nothing applies to a facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Measure time-of-service collection only against known, collectible patient responsibility, and track copay collection separately as an early-warning rate.
Treat pre-service coverage and benefit verification completion as the leading indicator; nothing is billed or collected correctly when coverage is unknown.
Segment the rate by responsibility type, visit type and staff member to separate process gaps from individual training gaps.
Pair firm collection with a written financial assistance policy and a patient-reported clarity question, so firmness does not turn into pressure.
red_flags: Collection-probability curve (95%, 70-80%, 50-60%, 30-40%) credited to unnamed research; contradicted by the same document's '40-60% at best' and by KPI 06.
Calls copays an 'absolute right' to collect at every visit; false for QMB and Medicaid patients, and silent on waiver limits, estimates and refunds.
Target shifts between 90% and 85%; verification standard shifts between 24 and 48 hours and between 80% and 85% completion.
No formula, full scripts, policy templates or cash-handling controls, despite pushing more money through the front desk; formula deferred to another product.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: KPI 06: Patient Collection Rate
summary: Vendor guide to total patient collection rate across point of service, statements, payment plans and agency. Diagnoses with a stage-by-stage funnel, then speeds and clarifies statements, adds payment plans and financial assistance, and makes agency referral rule-based. Built on commercial high-deductible economics; uncited statistics, a unit error, inconsistent deadlines and no Medicare, Medicaid or dual-eligible safeguards.
top_ideas: Build a stage-by-stage collection funnel on a date-of-service cohort to see whether dollars are lost at the visit, in statements, or at write-off.
Measure days from insurance adjudication to first patient statement by payer and generate statements automatically from electronic remittance posting.
Make agency referral rule-based with a documented final notice and a payment-plan offer first, adding the legal exclusions the document omits.
Trace ten random accounts end to end each quarter and watch complaints, so a rising rate reflects clarity rather than pressure.
red_flags: Says every dollar in the statement cycle costs '$8 to $15 to collect', a unit error; all effect sizes are uncited round ranges.
Orders referral to collections 'without exception', with no carve-out for QMB or Medicaid patients, bankruptcy, estates, disputes or pending secondary claims.
Three different statement-speed standards (21 days, 14 days, 3 business days) and phone and referral deadlines its own statement cadence cannot meet.
Assumes patient responsibility is 20-35% of revenue, later 25% of charges; wrong for a Medicare-heavy facility practice. Agency recovery of 20-35 cents looks optimistic.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: KPI 07: Write-Off Rate by Reason
summary: Thirty-page guide arguing that a practice's total write-off rate is useless until every adjustment carries a specific reason code. It separates contractual allowances, patient bad debt, timely-filing losses, denials whose appeal window lapsed, financial assistance and small balances; sets alarm levels for each (all unsourced); and labels timely-filing and expired-appeal losses 'preventable'. It follows the series' five steps: trigger thresholds;...
top_ideas: Require a specific reason code, from a fixed list, on every adjustment at the time it is posted.
Report avoidable losses (late filing, lapsed appeals, unresubmitted rejections) as their own dollar line every month and quarter.
Keep a payer-by-payer table of filing limits and appeal windows and drive alerts and queue order from it.
Stamp every denial with its appeal deadline at intake and work the queue by days to expiry.
red_flags: Recovery checklist suggests moving timely-filing or expired-appeal write-offs to patient responsibility. For Medicare a late filing is the provider's liability, QMB and Medicaid patients cannot be billed, and participating contracts...

Calls every timely-filing write-off 100% preventable and a pure process failure. Ignores retroactive eligibility, wrong coverage supplied by a facility, payer retro-terminations, and Medicare's recognized filing exceptions (administrative error, retroactive...
'A filed appeal stops the clock' is true only for that level; later levels carry their own limits. Medicare late-filing denials and unprocessable claims carry no appeal rights at all,...
The blanket 30-day appeal rule and the 30/45-day alerts imply short commercial-style windows (one example implies a 90-day filing limit). No real deadline is stated for any payer; Medicare's is...
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: KPI 08: Net Collection Rate
summary: Guide presenting net collection rate (payments divided by charges after contractual adjustments) as the master revenue-cycle metric. It gives five performance bands around a 97% target, warns that the figure depends on accurate contractual posting and is best measured by charge cohort, not period cash, and links it to the other series KPIs. The method is decomposition: compute the dollar...
top_ideas: Measure the rate by date-of-service cohort at fixed maturity points, alongside a rolling period figure.
Audit what is posted as contractual before trusting the rate.
Decompose the dollar gap into failure categories and rank them.
Compute the rate separately for each payer.
red_flags: The formula uses gross payments; standard definitions subtract refunds and recoupments. It never says which adjustments count as contractual, so payer 'contractual obligation' adjustments for late filing, bundling or missing...

States that Medicaid's lower rates make a lower rate structurally unavoidable. Under the document's own formula lower fee schedules are removed as contractual adjustments and cannot reduce the ratio; only...

The 97% 'achievable for any independent practice' target ignores cost-sharing that legally cannot be collected from dual-eligible (QMB) patients and that Medicaid often does not pay, and the 2% Medicare...

Patient responsibility 'commonly' at 20-35% of collectible revenue is unsourced and reflects high-deductible commercial populations; a Medicare, Medigap and dual-eligible panel has a far smaller true self-pay share, so the...
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: KPI 09: Charge Lag
summary: Defines charge lag (service date to charge entry) and treats it as a clinical-workflow problem. Offers threshold bands, three diagnostic pulls, a census-to-charge reconciliation, eight interventions, a 30-day sprint and monthly provider-level monitoring. Useful for rounding practices, but unsourced, surgery-heavy, and it includes one unsafe instruction to bill before documentation is complete.
top_ideas: Require same-day charge submission for every rounding visit and reconcile facility census or visit lists against posted charges, daily where possible, investigating every mismatch.
Report lag by provider and by care setting, not only the practice average, and put it on the provider scorecard beside RVUs and collections.
Trace five timestamps (service, note signed, received by billing, charge entered, claim submitted) to locate whether delay is clinical or billing-side.
Maintain a payer filing-deadline table and a weekly list of unbilled services approaching each deadline, built from actual contracts rather than generic 90/180/365 assumptions.
red_flags: Intervention 8 says to submit claims near the deadline regardless of documentation completeness; for Medicare this invites unsupported or false claims. Do not adopt.
No sources anywhere; thresholds, the 60-90 day relapse claim and dollar examples look invented. Timely-filing limits are generic, with no payer named.
Overstates deadline risk from a 3-5 day average lag and never measures the tail (charges weeks late or never entered) that actually causes write-offs.
Internal inconsistencies: provider trigger is 4 days in Section 0 but 3 in Section 5; reconciliation is daily in one place, monthly in another.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: KPI 10: Cost to Collect
summary: Defines cost to collect as fully loaded revenue-cycle cost over collections, paired with net collection rate. Gives bands (4-6% best practice), three diagnostics, a rework-then-staffing-then-technology sequence, quarterly tracking and a two-dimensional make-versus-buy test. Sound concepts, but benchmarks are unsourced, several numbers are wrong or inconsistent, and the staffing model ignores automated billing.
top_ideas: Calculate fully loaded cost to collect quarterly from a written cost-inclusion list, trend it year over year, and always read it next to net collection rate.
Sequence fixes: cut rework first, then judge capacity, then buy technology; track rework share of effort as the leading indicator.
Compare in-house versus vendor on two dimensions, all-in cost and reference-verified net collection rate; higher cost can win if it collects more.
Audit the whole revenue-cycle technology stack annually, tool by tool, for cost, function and measurable benefit.
red_flags: States collection agency commissions run about 1% of collections referred; contingency fees are normally a large double-digit share of recoveries. Wrong or garbled.
Small-balance rule ($25-$50, one statement, write off) ignores Medicare and Medicaid cost-sharing rules; in a Medicare facility practice it could amount to routine coinsurance waiver.
Benchmarks (4-6% best practice, 750-1,200 claims per FTE, rework multiples, cost shares) carry no source; thresholds conflict (4-6% target versus under-7% success signal).
Editing errors show no expert review: calls cost the 'denominator', says 40% is a 'majority', leaves a garbled self-correcting sentence and a meaningless scale-effect formula.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Annual Revenue Cycle Assessment Guide: A Comprehensive Self-Assessment Across 9 Revenue Cycle Domains
summary: A 48-page self-scoring checklist: 77 yes/no questions across nine revenue-cycle domains, a scorecard, rating bands and a blank action plan. It embeds about a dozen benchmark thresholds but gives no formulas, sources or workflows, repeats three pages verbatim, and routes low scorers to other paid products. Assumes an office practice with a front desk.
top_ideas: Run a data-backed revenue-cycle control review yearly, re-score quarterly, and fix the weakest domain first with one action, owner and 90-day target per gap.
Reconcile completed encounters to posted charges daily or weekly under a written charge-lag standard reported by provider.
Log a follow-up on every claim unpaid and undenied past a set age, and allow no write-off without a documented reason reviewed by category.
Compare remittances with expected allowed amounts quarterly to catch underpayments, and track denials by payer and reason code with a corrective action for each top reason.
red_flags: Scoring thresholds contradict each other: 7 of 9 is Strong in three domain rubrics but Moderate (77.8%) in the guide's own percentage key; no not-applicable option.
Dollar-loss ranges tied to score bands ($50,000-$150,000; $20K-$50K) and the 25-35% patient-responsibility figure have no source, method or scaling to practice size.
Coding currency is pegged to the 2021 office-visit E/M revision, ignoring the 2023 revision that governs hospital, nursing facility and home visits; audit questions look only for under-coding.

No-exceptions copay collection, mandatory-autopay plans and login-free balance display are scored as best practice with no mention of QMB and Medicaid limits, Regulation E or HIPAA identity verification.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Billing Department Performance Management Playbook: The System for Building, Managing, and Holding Accountable a Billing Team That Actually Performs
summary: Management primer for running a practice billing department by the numbers: three pillars (speed, accuracy, recovery), seven KPIs with formulas and targets, a review cadence, staffing and onboarding standards, weekly coaching, a five-step denial cycle, a six-stage workflow audit, owner oversight routine, vendor accountability and a 90-day turnaround plan. Benchmarks are unsourced and inconsistent; no regulatory or payer-specific content.
top_ideas: Fix one written formula per KPI and review on a set rhythm: daily volume and lag, weekly denials, monthly one-page scorecard with trends, quarterly benchmark review.
Pair each role or agent with one quality KPI and one timeliness KPI, and gate new workers through 100% review, then 25% spot-checks, then metric monitoring.
Run denials as a closed loop: log within 48 hours, categorize, trace to the upstream cause, rank by dollars, overturn odds and deadline, review any category rising two months.
Owner sets written outcome standards, holds a 20-minute monthly review with fixed questions, stays out of individual claims, and holds any vendor to identical KPI thresholds.
red_flags: Benchmarks credited to MGMA and HFMA carry no report or year and are stated two or three different ways; others rest on unverifiable 'CCRx-observed' experience.
The $300,000-plus gap on a $4M practice double-counts overlapping clean-claim and denial effects, treats delayed payment as lost revenue, and has no derivation despite being called documented.
Clean claim rate is defined to include payer denials, so it is not comparable with edit-stage benchmarks; formulas omit cohort, claim-versus-line and dollar rules.
Small-practice band (net collection 94-96%) conflicts with Section 2's rule that under 95% needs immediate analysis; no internal controls, compliance guardrails, payer rules or usable templates.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Charge Capture Audit Playbook: The Revenue You Earned But Never Billed
summary: Generic 44-page playbook on finding services delivered but never billed. Six failure points, a five-step audit (encounter reconciliation, 25-30 chart sample per provider, timely-filing denial review, bundling check, dollar quantification), four standing controls, three metrics, a 90-day plan and four checklists. Sound skeleton; unsourced thresholds; several coding examples are wrong; office and procedural bias.
top_ideas: Reconcile encounters delivered against charges posted every day, separately for each off-site location (hospital, nursing facility, assisted living, telehealth), and resolve every variance by the next business day.
Write a charge-lag standard per encounter type with a named owner and an escalation trigger; monitor lag by provider and location.
Require a logged reason and rule whenever a documented service is deliberately not billed, so bundling decisions can be sampled and corrected.
Trace each timely-filing denial back to provider, location and workflow step, and price audit findings in dollars at expected allowed amounts to drive action.
red_flags: Coding examples are wrong: there is no polypectomy add-on code; most office supplies and kits are bundled under Medicare; facility implants are not billable by the practice.

Calls timely-filing denials final absent administrative error; Medicare has further exceptions (retroactive entitlement, Medicare Advantage disenrollment) and other payers reverse them on proof of timely submission.
Only numeric justification, 1-5% of collectible revenue, is labelled 'HFMA-aligned' with no citation; every threshold (48/72 hours, 99%, 25-30 charts) is the vendor's own.
A skewed 25-30 chart sample is called statistically meaningful and extrapolated; audit only looks for underbilling, with no overpayment handling; nothing for census-based or time-based services.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: Coding Audit Playbook: The $50,000 to $150,000 Problem Hiding in Your Medical Records
summary: Vendor playbook for internal retrospective coding audits: risk-stratified sample of 25-30 records per provider, five-step review, four scorecards, four-tier risk rating, dollar extrapolation, audit calendar, provider education, policy outline and 90-day plan. Office-visit and surgery centric. Its E/M rubric and time table conflict with CPT, figures are unsourced, and the 60-day overpayment rule is absent.
top_ideas: Fixed audit calendar: annual full audit per provider, quarterly targeted re-audits for problem areas, trigger audits after code or policy changes, and a first-90-days audit for new providers.
Treat findings by direction: undercoding gets education and prospective fixes; overcoding triggers a stop-and-escalate path to counsel before any rebilling or repayment decision.
Give each clinician feedback from their own annotated charts: billed versus supported code, dollar impact, specific documentation fix, signed acknowledgment and a dated re-audit.
Screen each provider's visit-level distribution against specialty benchmarks before pulling charts, and test diagnoses both ways: conditions missed and codes the note does not support.
red_flags: E/M rubric contradicts CPT: invented additive point key, prescription management scored low risk (CPT: moderate), single data items scored extensive. It would flag correctly coded level-4 visits as overcoded.
Time table gives established codes 99212-99215 the new-patient ranges (15-29/30-44/45-59/60-74); CPT minimums are 10/20/30/40 minutes, and ranges were dropped in 2024.

Compliance section omits the 60-day overpayment report-and-return rule, misdescribes OIG self-disclosure as a routine overpayment channel, garbles OIG sample guidance, and extrapolates a non-random sample.

Unsourced $50K-$150K headline assumes every visit is undercoded; tells coders to prefer HCC-mapped codes; thresholds conflict (70% vs 90-95%); nothing on facility E/M, care management or wellness visits.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Denial Management Playbook: From Reactive Cleanup to Proactive Prevention
summary: Vendor playbook for running denials as both recovery and prevention: root-cause taxonomy, denial log, priority tiers, four-part appeals, deadline calendar, peer-to-peer prep, escalation ladder, monthly root cause analysis, pre-bill controls and benchmarked metrics. Sound but generic method; almost no sources, no denial-code detail or templates, and misleading legal statements on Medicare Advantage appeals, external review and parity.
top_ideas: Log every denial with a root-cause category and a computed appeal deadline at intake; sort work by deadline risk first, dollars second.
Run a monthly root cause review of top categories by dollars: what failed upstream, pattern or one-off, who owns it, what change removes it; assign dated actions.
Make scrubber edits a hard stop: no claim leaves with an unresolved edit unless a reasoned override is logged; add written prevention protocols per top payer.

Write medical-necessity appeals against the payer's own criteria, mapping chart evidence to each criterion; in Medicare Advantage appeals, cite Medicare coverage rules as the floor (verify scope first).
red_flags: Medicare Advantage escalation path (plan, independent review entity, Medicare ladder) is presented for all denials; contracted providers generally have only the contract's dispute process.

Legal overstatements: parity law said to require equal reimbursement rates; ACA external review and state insurance complaints treated as provider remedies with no ERISA, Medicare or patient-consent limits.

Statistics look invented or stale: unsourced denial-mix table with one-point ranges, uncited $25, $118 cost figure, unsourced benchmark targets; sole attribution 'MGMA DataDive and HFMA' has no report or year.

Medicare section omits reopenings, rejected-versus-denied claims, the judge-level dollar minimum and filing-limit exceptions, and muddles the one-year filing limit with appeal deadlines; no denial codes or templates anywhere.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Fee Schedule Optimization Playbook: The Number You Set Once and Never Looked at Again Is Costing You Money
summary: Argues a practice's charge list caps payment because payers pay the lower of charge or contract rate. Method: benchmark codes to Medicare, set charges at 200-250% of Medicare, audit code-by-payer gaps times volume, fix the charge master, update annually. Core idea sound; heavily repeated, unsourced, with a wrong net-collection-rate link. Weak fit for a Medicare-rate payer mix.
top_ideas: Treat the charge master as a ceiling control: every charge must exceed the highest allowable any payer has for that code, starting with the Medicare locality amount.
Automate a remittance exception: any paid line where allowed equals billed charge, with no contractual adjustment, means the charge is too low and gets reviewed.
Run an annual charge-master cycle tied to the Medicare final rule and CPT/HCPCS updates: add and retire codes, recalculate charges, load by January 1, keep a change log.
Reconcile services delivered against codes that exist with a charge, especially care-management and add-on codes; a missing code is worth more than re-pricing.
red_flags: Says under-set charges lower net collection rate and uses NCR as ROI; NCR is payments over allowed, so the loss cannot show there. Monitoring also confuses paid with allowed.
CY2026 factors expire December 31, 2026; CY2027 final rule cuts them to about $32.95/$32.63 (search-level check; cms.gov blocked in this session). '2023-2024 benchmarks understated' claim is false.
Omits Medicare limiting charge for non-participating physicians, usual-charge and self-pay disclosure rules; formula box uses one GPCI; facility settings defined as only hospital outpatient and ASC.
Every multiplier (200-250%, commercial 120-180%, workers' compensation over 300%) is unsourced; no author or citations; audit steps repeated four times; 'submit a test claim' advice is unsafe.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Medicare Advantage Operational Playbook
summary: Sixty-nine-page generic primer on running Medicare Advantage as separate commercial payers: authorization matrix and tracking, HCC capture with annual recapture, denial categories and appeals, claim checkpoints, contract inventory, carrier sketches, Stars and wellness visits, a dashboard and 90-day plan. Office-centric, almost uncited, and wrong on key coding, appeals and regulatory points; useful only as a skeleton.
top_ideas: One rule sheet per MA plan (authorization and referral rules, submission channel, timely-filing and dispute deadlines, modifier quirks) with a named owner and review date, wired into claim edits.
Document a one-line status for every chronic condition actually managed at a visit, track yearly recapture, and audit both missed and unsupported diagnoses under a written policy.
Classify MA denials by category and sub-type with a standard response for each, and have the treating clinician argue medical-necessity cases against the plan's stated criteria.
Abstract every MA contract into a term sheet, review each plan yearly on a scorecard, and vet any plan or vendor chart-review program before joining.
red_flags: ICD-10 examples are wrong (E11.65 is hyperglycemia, not diabetic CKD; I50.43 and I70.213 mislabeled) and I10 is said to carry HCC weight; V28 is never mentioned.
