Appeals table mislabels MA levels and presents the enrollee/non-contract CMS ladder as the practice's path; contracted-provider disputes follow the contract. Dollar thresholds are 2025 values.

Ignores 2024-2026 CMS rules: plans must follow Medicare coverage criteria, cannot retro-deny prior-authorized care for medical necessity (42 CFR 422.138(c)), and must decide standard requests in 7 days from 2026.
Unsourced round-number targets and scrubbed 'CCRx client data' claims; says payer price-transparency files show MA rates (they do not); Cigna profile ignores its 2025 MA sale.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Payer Rate Negotiation Playbook
summary: Vendor primer on raising commercial payer fee schedules: build a code-level rate table, benchmark against payer price-transparency files and published ratios, quantify dollar gap, document leverage, open nine to six months before renewal with a call, letter and data package, answer standard objections, bracket counteroffers, close in writing. Commercial-only; Medicare Advantage and Medicaid are not covered; most figures unsourced.
top_ideas: Maintain a per-payer code-level table for top codes (units, allowed, percent of locality Medicare), refreshed yearly; judge every proposed fee schedule against actual code mix, never an aggregate figure.
Run a contract calendar: each January set review, data and go/no-go dates 12, 10 and 9 months before every renewal and notice deadline.
Open via a named contact: call, then a letter with a specific code-level request; log every contact; confirm oral agreements in writing within 24 hours; attorney reviews amendments.
Fix the walk-away point before negotiating, never bluff termination, and ask for non-rate terms (escalator or current-year Medicare peg, prompt-pay, policy-change protection) alongside rates.
red_flags: Attributes payer machine-readable files to the No Surprises Act; the source is the 2020 Transparency in Coverage rule, which excludes Medicare Advantage and Medicaid, this practice's main negotiable payers.

Unverified or implausible numbers: Aroris 15.5% is vendor marketing; '2-3% increase = $500,000' needs $17-25 million from one payer; prompt-pay '1.5-2% per month' unsupported (Florida statute: 12% a year).

Outdated or contradictory: advice for Humana commercial, a business Humana exited; termination notice given as both 60-90 and 90-180 days; twelve-month timeline versus 90-day close; ignores 2026 conversion-factor increase.

No warning on contract confidentiality or antitrust when sharing other payers' rates or joining groups; omits fixed-year Medicare pegs, lesser-of clauses, rate-load verification, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid entirely.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Physician Compensation Negotiation Guide
summary: Employee-side primer for physicians evaluating an employment offer: benchmark base, model wRVU pay at three production levels, test bonus attainability, price tail coverage and non-compete, plan first-year cash, negotiate, then attorney review. No benchmark data, state law, citations or employer view. For an owner-employer it is useful mainly in reverse, as a hire-offer and post-sale agreement checklist.
top_ideas: Use the guide in reverse as an employer offer checklist: document answers on thresholds, bonus payout history, tail by termination scenario, modification rights and pay-calculation disputes before recruiting.
Model every provider pay plan at low, expected and high production using the practice's own wRVU history, showing provider pay and practice margin side by side.
Pay incentives as continuous per-wRVU rates, not cliffs, and define each quality metric with data source, payment date and an audit and dispute step.

Build a tail-coverage and restrictive-covenant term sheet: policy form, who pays tail in each termination scenario, mapped radius, duration, carve-outs and a pre-agreed buyout, with state-specific counsel.
red_flags: Calls an 85% to 95% net collection rate typical of a well-run practice; the conventional target is 95% or higher. Gross-rate range of 50% to 80% is arbitrary.
Non-compete advice has no state law and omits 2023-2025 statutes and the abandoned FTC rule; its construe-against-drafter claim contradicts Florida s. 542.335(1)(h).
Conversion-factor range ($45 to $65; $58 high-end for primary care) and every other dollar range are unsourced and appear stale; no benchmark values, citations, author or date.

Method contradicts itself: benchmarks base against MGMA total-compensation percentiles, glossary adds benefits to total compensation, and the greater-of worksheet cannot handle thresholds, tiers, cliffs, caps or draws.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Practice Financial Intelligence Playbook: The Financial Operating System for Independent Practices
summary: Capstone playbook linking revenue-cycle operations to practice finance: five-layer charge-to-cash waterfall, encounter break-even, service-line margins, 13-week cash forecast, capacity model, 14-metric dashboard, payer-mix economics, valuation drivers, growth modeling and a 30-60-90 rollout. Sound skeleton for an office-based practice; unsourced, internally inconsistent numbers and no usable templates.
top_ideas: Report a monthly charge-to-cash waterfall and state the allowed-minus-collected gap in dollars; review adjustment codes monthly for denials buried as contractual write-offs.
Keep a 13-week rolling cash forecast with every disbursement on its calendar date, refreshed weekly with actuals.
Compute break-even volume and contribution margin by service line, then classify each line as invest, optimize, monitor or exit.

Manage sale-readiness drivers continuously: provider revenue concentration, documented transferable processes, consistent monthly financials, stable revenue-cycle metrics and a clean compliance record.
red_flags: No citations; five embedded 'corrected/updated' notes show figures tuned to reconcile. Expense categories sum to 88-118% of net revenue against a 15-25% operating margin target.
Penalty figures stale or mixed: Stark at unindexed $15K-$100K, HIPAA cap at 2022-era $1.9M, False Claims Act mislabelled 'repayment + 3x penalties' with a 2024-25 range. Anti-Kickback absent.
Arithmetic errors: portal 'payback' of 1.4 days treats an AR balance as monthly cash; red flag 'below 85th percentile'; physician capacity 236 visits monthly versus 350 for an NP.
Valuation guidance never normalizes EBITDA for a market-rate owner salary or mentions fair-market-value limits; also silent on NP 85% payment, overpayment refund rule and credentialing lag.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Provider Compensation Design Playbook
summary: Primer on physician pay design: wRVU basics, MGMA/AMGA benchmarking, four model types, incentive domains, Stark fair-market-value framing, renegotiation, private-equity transactions, a written policy, 90-day plan and checklists. Sensible design principles, but uncited, physician-only, built on constructed benchmark numbers, and its Stark content is overstated or outdated in several places.
top_ideas: Before adopting any dollars-per-wRVU rate, compute its total cost at expected volume and confirm net revenue per wRVU, by payer and billing clinician, can fund it.
Pay production at one continuous rate with no cliffs or lump-sum thresholds, and audit coding before any incentive is calculated.
Keep a short written compensation policy, a one-page per-clinician summary that lets them recompute their pay, and a documented annual benchmark review.
Separate the owner's pay for clinical and management work from ownership profit so earnings can be normalized cleanly for valuation and sale.
red_flags: Stark section applies fair-market-value caps to practice owners and to every exception; its writing, one-year, holdover and 'absolute' volume/value statements look outdated or wrong.
Benchmark figures are constructed, not sourced: $45-$65 per wRVU and a $220,500 primary-care median, back-solved from each other, sit well below recent survey levels.
No citations, survey year, author or regulation references; ignores 2021-2026 fee-schedule changes to wRVU values that reshape any wRVU-based pay plan.

Physician-only despite the 'Provider' title: nothing on nurse practitioner pay, facility-based work, care-management credit or owner-pay tax treatment; its tier example recreates the cliff it warns against.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Revenue Cycle Technology Buyer's Playbook: What Vendors Don't Show You in the Demo
summary: Generic buyer's guide for EHR/PM, clearinghouse and patient-payment software: probe demos on exception workflows, demand customer-base performance data, use independent references, score vendors on a 12-row scorecard, negotiate ten vendor-favoring clauses and exit terms, review 90 days post-go-live. Unsourced; omits HIPAA, security, information-blocking, AI and cost-of-ownership content; patient-portal emphasis misfits a facility-based Medicare practice.
top_ideas: Keep a contract register for every vendor (cost, term, renewal-notice deadline, escalator) and calendar each notice date with a buffer on the day of signing.
Make vendors demonstrate exception paths (eligibility errors, clearinghouse rejections, denials) and run named KPI reports live, using the practice's own scenarios rather than the happy path.
Review fixed clause types with counsel before signing or renewing: data ownership and export, price-increase cap, liability cap, termination for cause, unilateral modification, rights in custom work.
Use independent references and a 90-day post-go-live review against a pre-implementation baseline, repeated at 6, 12 and 24 months against benchmarks recorded at signing.
red_flags: Every statistic is unsourced and several look invented or inconsistent: 25-35% patient share of revenue, 7-10 year EHR tenure, $5,000-$50,000+ migration, and 72%/85%/60%/70% patient-payment figures.

Omits HIPAA business associate terms, security diligence, information-blocking and EHI-export rights, AI data use, total cost of ownership and clearinghouse contingency; data-export advice reads as pre-Cures-Act.

Conflates clearinghouse rejections with payer denials, credits the clearinghouse with first-pass performance, and treats prior-authorization requirements in real-time eligibility responses as a minimum standard despite unreliable payer data (verify).

Shaky contract advice: 180-day auto-renewal 'window' is ambiguous or backwards; the 12-month liability cap sought looks like the market default (verify); only three of five named categories get frameworks.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Credentialing and Re-Credentialing Management Playbook
summary: Calendar-driven system for provider credentialing and payer enrollment: one named owner, a provider-by-payer calendar with internal triggers, a live tracker with payer follow-up every two weeks, a 72-hour gap protocol, a six-domain audit and five KPIs. The process skeleton is sound; rule detail is unsourced, partly wrong or outdated, and omits Medicare Advantage, nurse practitioners and facility privileging.
top_ideas: Keep one provider-by-payer calendar for every expiring item (plan re-credentialing, CAQH attestation, Medicare revalidation, licence, DEA, malpractice) with internal triggers set well ahead of each deadline.
Re-attest CAQH on a 90-day internal cycle and upload renewed documents the day they renew, so the profile is never expired when a payer pulls it.
Pull Medicare revalidation due dates from the CMS list on a schedule instead of waiting for a notice; a missed revalidation means deactivation and unpaid services.
Run a live application tracker with payer contact every two weeks and a logged trail, and confirm individual-to-group linkage at each payer before the first claim.
red_flags: Says file Medicare enrollment 90 to 120 days before start; CMS may return practitioner applications received more than 60 days before the listed effective date.
Q6 locum rule misdescribed as billing under a 'supervising physician'; omits the 60-day limit and that it covers substitute physicians only, not nurse practitioners.

No sources; stale or unverified specifics: 'CAQH ProView' name, CMS-855R form, PECOS 2.0 login claims, '18 data sections', a UnitedHealthcare 14-day attestation rule, blanket no-retroactivity for Medicaid.
Internal errors: four unbillable months said to yield 33% of revenue; UnitedHealthcare timeline given as both 60-90 and 45-90 days; Metric 3 contradicts Section 4's six-month trigger.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: New Practice Launch Playbook: Build the Revenue Cycle Right the First Time
summary: Start-up guide for physicians opening an office-based independent practice: a ten-step, lead-time-ordered build sequence, pre-opening enrollment and technology setup, a four-month cash reserve worksheet, early claim and coding habits, month-3/6/12 checkups and a 42-item checklist. Unsourced, office-centric, and wrong or outdated on several Medicare enrollment rules; low direct value to an established facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Run enrollment as a tracked pipeline per clinician and payer: panel check, biweekly follow-up, response-deadline alarms, 120-day CAQH re-attestation, and a dollar-valued hold-and-bill log for pending payers.
Sequence any launch (clinician, site, plan) by external lead time and dependency, starting the slowest approvals first, using corrected Medicare filing and effective-date rules.
Test every charge against the highest amount any payer actually allows each year, because payers pay the lesser of charge or allowable.
Pair each ramp KPI with a pre-agreed response at fixed milestones, and audit a new clinician's coding at about 90 days with a small record sample.
red_flags: Says Medicare can be filed only 30 days before opening; contractor (First Coast) guidance returns applications only beyond 60 days. Its own checklist says file 90 days ahead.
Cites the CMS-855R, discontinued in 2023, and says every new practice needs both 855I and 855B; a sole-owner entity can generally enroll on the 855I alone.

Says not to see Medicare patients until approval and that pending payers are unbillable, ignoring filing-date effective dates and the 30-day look-back; contradicts its own retroactive-billing checklist.

No sources or author; hardship-policy risk blamed on HIPAA instead of kickback and inducement law; 'copays without exception' ignores QMB protections; reserve worksheet omits owner pay and volume ramp.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Patient Collections Playbook: Stop Sending Statements Into the Void
summary: Vendor playbook for office practices: collect patient cost-sharing at scheduling, check-in and checkout using scripts, then autopay payment plans, a 90-day multichannel statement ladder, hardship screening, three monthly targets and a 13-week rollout. Conventional workflow skeleton, but unsourced, formula-free and silent on Medicare, Medicaid, dual-eligible and consumer-credit rules. Poor fit for a facility-based Medicare practice.
top_ideas: Dated patient-balance ladder: first statement 7-10 days after final adjudication, text, second statement, call over $100, final notice at day 60, forced disposition by day 75-90.

Written financial assistance policy: income-based criteria, decision in five business days, written notice, documented and audited, rebuilt around the federal hardship exception for Medicare cost-sharing.
Structured payment plans with a minimum, autopay, written terms and payoff date, after legal review of installment-credit and bank-draft rules.

Monitor patient receivables separately each month (collection rate, receivable days, plans, agency referrals) from a recorded baseline, with formulas written and legally uncollectible dual-eligible cost-sharing excluded.
red_flags: 'No exceptions' copay-before-rooming and check-in balance collection ignores QMB, Medicaid and VA billing prohibitions; Medicare, Medicaid and dual-eligibles are never mentioned.
Every statistic is unsourced: 25-35% of revenue from patients, 20-30 cents agency recovery, 90%+ text open rates, 60-75% versus 90% collection. Several conflict with published data.

Payment plan and hardship advice omits Truth in Lending, Regulation E, the federal cost-sharing waiver exception and No Surprises Act estimate rules; the 'tax-advantaged' charity write-off remark is misleading.
Three headline metrics have targets but no formulas; the under-30-day patient receivable target conflicts with the document's own 90-day ladder and 10-20 month plans.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Practice Acquisition Revenue Cycle Integration Playbook: The Operational Blueprint for Due Diligence, Day-One Continuity, and Full RC Integration
summary: A buy-side guide to keeping a physician practice's revenue cycle intact through an acquisition and then improving it. It follows the deal clock: a seven-area diligence review (collection trends, receivable quality, payer contracts, credentialing, billing staff, compliance history, technology); turning findings into price through a collection-rate gap estimate and age-bucket discounting of receivables; pre-close workstreams starting roughly 90 days out;...
top_ideas: Use the seven diligence areas as an annual sale-readiness self-audit and keep the 24 requested documents current in a standing data room.
Keep a payer contract and enrollment register: contracting entity, tax ID and NPI linkage, effective and renewal dates, assignment and change-of-control terms, fee schedule, pay-to address.
Value receivables at net realizable value by payer and age bucket using the practice's own liquidation history, never at face value.
In an asset deal, default to the seller keeping pre-close receivables so the buyer starts with a clean ledger.
red_flags: Medicare gap is mischaracterized. The text says claims under the new entity are rejected for 30-90 days and suggests pricing that as lost revenue or 'negotiating a retroactive billing arrangement'....
Advice to file PECOS 90+ days before close (timeline: applications in by T-75) collides with CMS enrollment processing rules: a contractor may return a CMS-855B or 855I received more than...
Medicare section never separates an equity purchase (same tax ID and enrollment; ownership change reportable within 30 days under 42 CFR 424.516(d)) from an asset purchase with a new tax...
The blanket ban on billing under the seller's credentials is right for a new-tax-ID asset deal but is stated without the equity-deal case, and the False Claims Act label is...
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Practice Closure and Wind-Down Revenue Cycle Playbook
summary: Vendor playbook framing practice closure or sale as a revenue-cycle project: a 12-24 month reverse timeline covering receivables acceleration, payer and Medicare exit, patient notice, record retention, tail coverage, a final coding audit, receivables sale and knowledge transfer, with checklists. Useful as a topic list; several regulatory statements are wrong and its timelines conflict. No templates or sources.
top_ideas: Plan any exit backward from a fixed date, with a standing register of every payer, facility and vendor notice term; the longest term sets the start.
Fund a 12-18 month billing run-out after the last date of service: keep systems, bank account, remittance enrollments and mail routing alive.
Keep a retention schedule and portable archive of clinical and billing data (ten-year working standard), plus a documented pre-exit coding audit as the audit-defense and diligence file.
Document billing operations, credentials and system settings so billing survives loss of a key person; write an emergency plan for an unplanned stop.
red_flags: Says the Medicare 90-day withdrawal clock starts at the decision to close; CMS ties it to actually retiring or leaving. The playbook's own schedules then contradict each other.
Offers 'accept the audit risk' as an option after finding overpayments and points to the Stark disclosure protocol; never mentions the 60-day report-and-return rule.
Claims Medicare pays in 60-90 days (clean electronic claims pay in about 14); cites a HIPAA security section as the record-retention rule; North Carolina row is a hospital rule.

No templates, sources or named author; statistics are 'CCRx-observed' with no data; outdated references (2021 visit-level guidelines, CAQH ProView); nothing on facilities, Medicare Advantage or Florida closure rules.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Practice Valuation and Revenue Cycle Readiness Playbook: What a Buyer Sees in Your Revenue Cycle Before You Do
summary: Seller-side guide to preparing a practice's revenue cycle for buyer diligence: capitalize sustainable EBITDA gains, self-audit KPIs, coding, AR, contracts and compliance, document workflows, build a data room over 12 months. Sound outline; numbers unsourced, protocols deferred to nine sibling products, several legal points wrong or incomplete, and not written for small, facility-based, Medicare-heavy practices.
top_ideas: Run the buyer's diligence on yourself annually: KPI trends, code-distribution screen, AR aging and collectibility, contract inventory, compliance log; fix findings while you still control the timeline.
Write a billing operations manual and keep 24-36 months of month-end reports so the revenue cycle is a transferable, documented system, including the AI-agent workflows.
Present improvement honestly: separate one-time AR recoveries from sustainable run-rate, document every add-back, and value receivables by age at a discount rather than face.
Learn the deal mechanics early: working-capital target and true-up, who keeps pre-close AR, escrow for compliance representations, and how transition costs can erode earnout EBITDA.
red_flags: Overpayments: frames repayment as optional self-disclosure and says corrected coding 'has addressed the exposure'; omits the mandatory 60-day report-and-return duty, lookback, and FCA per-claim penalties.
Outdated or wrong technical details: deleted CPT 99201 listed as current, 'Stark Law safe harbors', muddled 'Medicare Advantage ACO'; Medicare denial priorities ignore the 120-day appeal window.
Core deal math is muddled: AR cleanup 'pays twice', a higher working-capital target is treated as good for the seller, and 7x examples contradict its own 3-5x small-practice range.

Every number is unsourced except one two-firm citation; no KPI formulas, no templates, protocols deferred to nine other products; nothing on owner-compensation normalization, tax, Medicare enrollment or facility-based billing.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: RCM Outsourcing Evaluation Playbook: Before You Hand Over the Keys to Your Revenue Cycle
summary: Buyer-side guide to outsourced billing: model choice, vendor types and fees, due diligence, six contract clauses, eight KPI floors, monthly and quarterly oversight, a three-level escalation ladder and a 90-day exit plan. Useful oversight skeleton; numbers are uncited, KPI definitions loose, billing-agent law absent, and one credentialing workaround is hazardous. The method transfers to AI-run in-house billing.
top_ideas: Recompute billing KPIs monthly from the practice's own system under written definitions and reconcile to whatever the billing operator, human or AI, reports.
Put each KPI's formula, floor, measurement window and breach consequence in writing, then convert every shortfall into monthly and annual dollars before acting.
Review every write-off monthly, separating contractual adjustments from avoidable administrative losses, with a reason and owner sign-off for the avoidable kind.
Keep ownership of system, data and credentials; benchmark in-house all-in cost to collect against outsourced pricing; use a time-boxed, documented escalation ladder for any vendor or agent failure.
red_flags: Offers billing an uncredentialed clinician under a supervising provider's NPI as a routine workaround; for Medicare hospital and nursing-facility visits that is false-claims exposure.

No source for any number. The disclaimer says figures are labeled benchmark or vendor-observed; none is. Fee ranges, aging collectability factors and credentialing timelines look invented or untraceable.
KPI definitions are loose or contradictory: days in AR defined non-standardly with no formula; 95% clean-claim floor conflicts with 8% denial ceiling; NCR floor is 94% and 96%.

Omits the legal core of outsourced billing: percentage-fee agent payment rules, practice liability for vendor claims, exclusion screening, offshore data, cyber continuity, overpayment refunds; calls audit non-response an 'admission'.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Revenue Cycle Staffing & Compensation Playbook: What to Pay, How to Structure, and How to Know When It's Working
summary: Vendor playbook on staffing a practice's billing office with people: role definitions, behavioral hiring tests, unsourced 2025 pay ranges with adjustment factors, incentive do's and don'ts, team structures by size, a build/buy/outsource comparison, role KPIs, a weekly/monthly/quarterly review rhythm, retention levers, a departure knowledge audit and an annual pay review. Sound frameworks; numbers unsourced and inconsistent across sections.
top_ideas: Scorecard every billing function (charge entry, posting, denials, receivables follow-up, coding) with a target and an intervention threshold, whether a person, vendor or AI agent does the work.
Fixed management rhythm: 30-minute weekly check of denials, charge lag and posting; monthly KPI, aging and write-off review; quarterly half-day review of trends, structure and tools.
Reward quality ratios, never raw collections, claim counts or recovered-denial dollars, and publish the criteria before the year starts; applies equally to vendor fees and agent objectives.
At every handoff, audit undocumented know-how (custom system workflows, payer quirks, recurring tasks, escalation contacts, working files); require a documented decision for every write-off.
red_flags: No source, sample or method for any pay figure; 'medians' are ranges dated 2025; Section 12 contradicts Sections 4-5 on manager pay, certification and remote premiums.
Turnover cost of 50-100% of salary is unsourced; published reviews put the median near 20% for jobs under $50,000, so the retention-bonus math is likely overstated two- to five-fold.
Uses the 'CPC-H' credential, renamed COC in January 2015, and ties it to DRG work; 'E&M within 10% of specialty norm' is an undefined, unrecognized coding standard.

Silent on overtime treatment of bonuses, exclusion screening, access revocation at departure, internal controls, Medicare limits on percentage-paid billing agents and automated billing; closing note cites nonexistent labels.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Telehealth Revenue Cycle Playbook: The Billing Rules Changed. Did Your Workflow?
summary: Medicare-centric telehealth billing playbook: sorts rules into permanent, temporary (through 31 Dec 2027) and expired; covers POS 02/10, modifiers, audio-only, payer-type differences; then a six-step lookback audit and 90-day fix plan. Largely current on 2026 law but unsourced, with coding and history errors, a hollow payer section, and no overpayment guidance. Marginal for a facility-based practice.
top_ideas: Keep a rule-status register tagging each billing rule permanent, temporary with expiry date, or expired, and calendar every sunset date.
Maintain a payer-by-payer rules matrix (codes, POS, modifiers, audio-only, prior auth, last-verified date) and drive claim logic from it rather than one system default.
Audit a baseline before changing workflow, then re-measure the same error and denial rates; triage errors into correctable and not, never backfilling documentation.
Keep care-management codes (CCM, RPM) outside telehealth POS/modifier logic; chart patient location and modality in every telehealth note.
red_flags: Worked example miscodes a new patient with 30 minutes and low MDM as 99202 (should be 99203); tables pair modifier 93 with POS 02, contradicting the home-only audio rule.
'44 states plus D.C.' parity figure conflates coverage laws with payment parity; the 10-25% POS differential is unsourced and looks understated; no citations anywhere.
Audit covers only errors that underpay; silent on overpayment-direction errors and the 60-day report-and-return duty; conflates timely filing with Medicare reopening.
History wrong for Medicare (POS 11 'ended May 2023', GT 'used during PHE', 99441-99443 a 'PHE construct'); RPM/CCM code lists incomplete for 2026; predates CY 2027 fee-schedule rule.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Value-Based Care Revenue Cycle Implications Playbook
summary: Treats value-based payments (MIPS, ACO shared savings, Medicare Advantage risk adjustment, PCMH fees) as a second revenue stream the billing team should own. Method: inventory programs, measure standing, close gaps, then run a monthly value-based report with separate financial lines. Rules keyed to 2026; several MIPS details are outdated or wrong, and dollar examples are uncited and inconsistent.
top_ideas: Run MIPS as penalty avoidance: exposure is up to 9% of Medicare Part B payments two years later; aim for the 75-point threshold and budget bonuses at 1-2%.

Monthly value-based scorecard (estimated MIPS score, wellness-visit completion, chronic-condition recapture, payer or ACO quality standing, deadlines within 90 days), with these revenues booked on separate lines.
Two-way diagnosis-support audits folded into the coding audit: remove unsupported conditions as well as add missed ones, under qualified coder oversight.
Read ACO and risk contracts for attribution, minimum savings rate, sharing rate, downside, distribution formula and absolute versus relative benchmarks before signing.
red_flags: MIPS rules wrong or stale: MVP registration timing, improvement-activity weighting, quality bonus points, eCQM 'flat benchmarks'; claims-based reporting and ACO attribution (tax ID, not NPI) mischaracterized.
Risk-adjustment dollar math contradicts itself by roughly four to ten times across three sections, ignores prospective payment timing, and treats plan capitation as practice revenue.

V28 advice uses V24 logic (diabetes complications no longer raise the weight); 'definitive drug testing into HCC mapping' appears invented; RADV extrapolation presented without its 2025 court vacatur.
No sources; 'CCRx has observed' numbers unverifiable; 'no APM bonus under current law' and ACO REACH content may be overtaken by 2026 changes; nothing on facility-based practice.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Front-End Revenue Cycle Playbook: The Complete Operational Playbook for Independent Practice
summary: Vendor playbook for office-based practices covering registration, eligibility, insurance discovery, prior authorization, desk collections, financial counseling, scheduling intake, six front-end KPIs and staffing. Method: capture and re-verify fixed data at every visit, then trace denials back to intake quarterly. Conventional and mostly sound, but unsourced, internally inconsistent, thin on regulation, and without usable forms or templates.
top_ideas: Treat eligibility as a required-field check (coverage dates, cost share, network, referral and authorization rules, payer order, limits, Medicare secondary status) and store the full response as evidence.
Each quarter, trace every denial and rejection to the intake step that caused it; report the front-end share as the baseline and review by operator monthly.
Adopt a written hardship and financial assistance policy with a documented individual determination each time; never waive Medicare cost-sharing routinely.
Search for coverage, with a separate Medicaid query, whenever coverage is unverifiable or lapsed, and re-verify on a schedule and before releasing any held claim.
red_flags: No author, date or citations; every statistic (20-30% hidden coverage, 50-65% administrative authorization denials, $8-$14 per statement, 15-40% collection cost) is unsourced or rests on unverifiable vendor experience.

Compliance statements are imprecise: routine waiver labeled a False Claims Act violation, 'balance billing' misused; nothing on Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, good-faith estimates, ABNs, timely filing or Truth in Lending.

Internal contradictions: nine elements promised, seven given; eligibility timing 48 versus 48-72 hours; Medicare Advantage matrix quarterly versus monthly; collection-rate tiers conflict; discovery threshold versus every self-pay patient.

Built for a staffed front desk; ignores 2024-2026 federal prior-authorization rules, uses retired payer names, and supplies no forms, scripts or templates despite being sold as a complete operational playbook.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Payer Contract Intelligence Playbook: How to Read, Negotiate, and Manage Payer Contracts in Independent Practice
summary: Guide to reading, benchmarking, negotiating, terminating and administering payer contracts. Method: express each payer's top-25-code rates as a percentage of Medicare, cost out each payer, build leverage, negotiate in writing, verify payments. Sound skeleton, but commercial and office-based in outlook, unsourced, with wrong or missing rules for Medicare, Medicare Advantage, prompt payment, credentialing and out-of-network billing.
top_ideas: Keep a contract registry with dates, notice periods, prompt-pay and amendment terms, reviewed monthly, and log every payer notice with its response deadline.
Build a payer-by-code matrix of allowed amounts as a percentage of local Medicare for the top 25 codes; use it to target negotiations.
Check remittances against contracted rates (every line, not a 20-30 claim sample) and dispute systematic shortfalls; recheck loaded rates after each amendment.
Rank payers by cost-to-serve and burden as well as rate; screen value-based offers on data capability, workflow and downside risk.
red_flags: Out-of-network and termination advice ignores the No Surprises Act, Medicare limiting-charge and opt-out rules, Medicare Advantage non-contract payment at Medicare rates, and Medicaid and dual-eligible billing bans.
Termination formula is incoherent (four inputs, three used, sign points the wrong way); underpayment test compares paid amount, not allowed amount, with the contract rate.
Prompt-pay section gives generic 30-45 day deadlines and omits that state laws skip self-funded plans, Medicare and contracted Medicare Advantage claims; Florida's are 20 and 40 days.
Benchmarks unsourced; the 'over 250%' figure is a hospital facility ratio, not physician fees; '130 percent of billed charges' example is nonsensical; credentialing 'on day one' is too late.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Prior Authorization Management Playbook: Stop Letting the Payer's Friction Win
summary: Generic prior-authorization workflow primer for scheduled, procedural practices: three cost layers, five failure points, a six-field tracking register with 14-day expiry alerts, peer-to-peer preparation and scripts, a labor and lost-revenue worksheet, payer profiles, three metrics and a 90-day rollout. Cites no regulations; numbers are unsourced vendor estimates. Limited fit for a facility-based geriatrics practice.
top_ideas: Keep one authorization record per patient per service: submission and receipt dates, expiry with 14-day alert, defined status, one named owner, documented outcome. Review the list daily.
Triage every denial: administrative ones are fixed and resubmitted within 48 hours; clinical ones get a physician-level decision on challenge. No denial is written off without that review.

Build a per-payer profile (turnaround, approval rate, denial reasons, validity window, extension and expedited rules, best channel, escalation contact) and set submission lead times and documentation checklists from it.
Prepare peer-to-peer calls with a one-page packet: the payer's cited criteria, chart facts, a named guideline, three to five talking points; afterward record reviewer name, credential and rationale.
red_flags: Ignores 2026 federal decision deadlines (7 calendar days standard, 72 hours expedited for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care); still scripts '7 to 14 business days'.
Dollar ranges, the 8-12% drop-off 'industry estimate' and the 80% and 60% targets are unsourced; the cost worksheet double counts cancellations and treats delayed revenue as lost.
Peer-to-peer is presented as always available after denial, with no deadlines; Humana and Wellcare Medicare plans reportedly no longer let a post-denial call change the decision.
Lists defunct vendor Olive; three cross-references point to the wrong section; calls never-billed revenue the largest layer while its own table shows labor larger in every specialty.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Insider News 01: The Insider, Issue 01: Your Billing Software Isn't Broken. Your Configuration Is.
summary: Undated opinion essay (archive index: March 31, 2026), no news. Argues high denials usually reflect untouched system configuration, not bad software: generic scrubber edits, no contracted fee schedules loaded, no worklist routing by denial code. Offers one audit: map the top five denial codes of 90 days to missing or broken edits. No sources, systems, codes or evidence.
top_ideas: Rank denial reason codes for the trailing 90 days and, for each, decide whether a pre-submission check could have stopped it; then build or repair that check.
Load an expected allowed amount per payer and code so every payment is compared with what was owed and short payments surface.
Route denials to separate worklists by reason category with defined follow-up instead of one mixed queue.
Before replacing a system, test whether recurring denials could be prevented with features already owned; also test rules that exist but failed to fire.
red_flags: No date on the page (archive index: March 31, 2026) and no news: no rule, deadline or announcement; an evergreen sales essay with zero sources.
Its one diagnostic is false: many denials (coverage changes, hospice, coordination of benefits, authorization, medical necessity) cannot be prevented by claim edits.
Unsupported numbers: two or three denial codes removed by one setting change, revenue impact in 30 days, a three-hour fix.
Claims all systems ship with generic rules only, ignoring vendor and clearinghouse edits. Names no system, payer or code; fee schedule loading and denial routing get no instructions.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Insider News 02: The Insider, Issue 02: Your Payer Sent You a Letter. You Filed It. That Was Your Consent.
summary: Undated opinion essay (archive index: April 14, 2026), no news. Warns that payer contracts let the payer change rates and rules by written notice, with silence through a 30-90 day window treated as acceptance. Recommends one owner for payer mail, a log, calendared deadlines, written objections and a remittance drift check. Legal claims are unqualified and unsourced.
top_ideas: One named owner for every payer communication across mail, email, portals and bulletins, so nothing is filed unread.
Payer communications log with date received, change described, effective date, response deadline and action taken; calendar the deadline the day it is logged.
Monthly check of paid amounts per high-volume code per payer; investigate any step change after ruling out the annual Medicare fee schedule update.
Inventory each contract's amendment clause in advance (notice period, objection and termination rights) and keep a revenue-impact file for renegotiation.
red_flags: 'This is legal' with no jurisdiction; state laws on material contract changes and Medicare Advantage or Medicaid plan rules are ignored. Florida's rule needs checking.
Confuses credentialing with contracting: calls the 'next credentialing renewal' the negotiation point. Recredentialing is a verification cycle, not a rate negotiation.
The example's timeline is impossible: change effective about a week ago, yet payments 9% low for three months. Subhead says every contract, body says almost every commercial one.
No news: undated on the page (archive index: April 14, 2026), no source, no sample letter or log; advises disputing without warning that objection can trigger termination.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Insider News 03: The Insider, Issue 03: The Patient Balance Conversation Nobody Has
summary: Undated opinion essay (archive index: April 28, 2026), no news. Claims practices collecting at check-in get 60 to 80 percent of patient responsibility versus 34% in its example; prescribes early eligibility checks and three scripted conversations. Numbers are unsourced and legal limits on collecting from Medicare and Medicaid patients are ignored. Barely applies here.
top_ideas: Verify eligibility and benefits before every encounter; for facility work, at admission and monthly, to catch plan switches, hospice election and QMB status.
Measure patient responsibility collection rate (collected divided by billed) by payer type, excluding amounts that may not legally be billed.
Ask for payment at the earliest moment the amount is known; without a check-in, use a financial agreement and payment authorization at onboarding.
Size the opportunity with a two-line calculation on actual patient responsibility before building any collection program, using a sourced target rate.
red_flags: 60-80% and 'conservative' 70% collection rates are unsourced and applied to all patient responsibility, including amounts unknown until the claim adjudicates.
Omits every legal limit: QMB and Medicaid billing prohibitions, Medicare over-collection refunds, good-faith estimates for self-pay. Dangerous as written for a geriatric practice.
Check-in premise does not fit a facility-based practice with no front desk; near-zero direct applicability.
No news, no date on the page (archive index: April 28, 2026). Vendor's archive blurb says most practices run 34%; the issue calls 34% not normal.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Insider News 04: Today Is the Day the Old ABN Form Dies
summary: Deadline alert: the renewed Medicare ABN form (CMS-R-131) became mandatory May 12, 2026 after a 60-day changeover. Explains the notice's purpose, three common errors (old version, late signature, use outside Original Medicare) and three same-day actions. Date corroborated by secondary sources; scope and legal effect are overstated; no modifiers, citations or tools.
top_ideas: Keep a register of mandated patient notices with version identifier, source link, install date and next renewal, and check it on a schedule.
Gate ABN use on payer type: Original Medicare only; Medicare Advantage members need the plan's own coverage determination.
Deliver the notice before the service with time to decide; never afterwards and never as a blanket waiver.
Look back at Medicare medical-necessity and frequency denials and check each for a valid notice and the right modifier.
red_flags: Says an ABN is required for any non-covered or excluded service; for statutory exclusions it is voluntary and the patient can be billed without one.
Absolute wording ('legally unenforceable', 'not appealable') overstates: the denial stays appealable, and secondary sources differ on May 12 versus May 13.
Tells staff to find a form 'dated March 2026'; the form is identified by its OMB expiration date (reported as 03/31/2029).
No modifiers, dual-eligible or representative-signature guidance and no citation; 'courts have consistently held' is unsourced; the tools sit behind a paid product.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Insider News 05: Federal IDR: What's Actually Changing
summary: How-to pitch for No Surprises Act arbitration: an 80% provider win rate, a $115 fee, the pending QPA lawsuit, four 'statutory factors' and a 90-day remittance screen. It misses the final rule published five days earlier, misstates negotiation timing and two factors, and omits arbitrator fees and scope limits. Almost irrelevant to this practice's payer mix.
top_ideas: Do expected-value arithmetic before any dispute or appeal: recovery times realistic odds, minus all fees and staff time.
Screen remittances on a schedule for payments below the expected amount, using a claim-type filter plus a dollar threshold.
In final-offer arbitration submit the figure most likely to be chosen, not the highest defensible one.
Keep a dated watch list of rulemaking and litigation built from primary sources, and keep meeting running deadlines meanwhile.
red_flags: Dated June 9, 2026 yet ignores the IDR Operations final rule published June 4; its $115 fee reportedly fell to $15 on June 11.
Open-negotiation timing is wrong: 30 business days from when the notice is sent, itself due within 30 business days of payment; 'you can still file' misleads.
Two of four 'statutory factors' are misstated, and the cost math omits the arbitrator fee the losing party forfeits.
States no scope limits: the process excludes Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, VA, Tricare and non-hospital settings, so it barely touches this practice.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Insider News 06: The Timely Filing Clock: What It Is, When It Runs Out, and How to Stop the Bleed
summary: Evergreen how-to on filing deadlines with no news: typical limits by payer type, four exposure points (rejections, secondary claims, eligibility errors, credentialing delays), a daily-rejection and deadline-flag workflow, triage for aged claims and a weekly audit. Workflow is sound; legal statements are partly wrong (contract-not-law, Medicaid 24 months, denial finality).
top_ideas: Work every clearinghouse and payer front-end rejection the day it appears, with one named owner.
Stamp each claim with its payer-specific filing deadline at creation, and the secondary deadline when the primary is sent.
Flag aging claims by share of filing window used (60/80/90%) plus a days-remaining floor, and escalate the last tier to a human.
Maintain a sourced, dated payer limit table covering initial, corrected, secondary and appeal windows; code late-filing write-offs by root cause.
red_flags: 'Set by contract, not by law' is wrong: Medicare's one-year limit is statutory and federal rules cap Medicaid filing at 12 months.
Medicaid range of 'up to 24 months' conflicts with the 12-month federal ceiling for initial claims.
Blurs rejections with denials, which usually have separate correction and appeal windows; says denials are final, then offers an exception route.
Offers patient billing after late filing and mentions billing under another provider's NPI without the compliance warnings both need; no news content or sources.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: Insider News 07: PA Rules Changed. Here's Your New Workflow.
summary: How-to issue claiming federal prior authorization rules changed on 1 January 2026 (72-hour urgent and 7-day standard payer decisions, mandatory FHIR electronic authorization) and turning that into desk routines: log submission dates, flag urgent requests, check vendor support, document late responses. Names the rule but omits which payers are covered and states the electronic duty a year early.
top_ideas: Keep a provable submission record (date, channel, payer reference number) for every authorization request so a missed payer deadline can be shown.
Run expedited requests on a separate flagged path with written clinical urgency criteria.
Set an internal reminder two days before the payer's decision deadline and log deadline misses by plan.
Ask EHR and clearinghouse vendors what electronic authorization they support now and for the January 2027 payer interface deadline.
red_flags: Says payers must already support FHIR electronic prior authorization; the federal API compliance date is January 1, 2027.
Applies the 72-hour and 7-day limits to all payers; they bind only Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP plans, exclude drugs, and never touch commercial plans or traditional Medicare.
Says the rule was finalized January 1, 2026; it was issued January 2024. Also wrong that no decision timelines existed before 2026.
Relies on an unnamed CMS complaint mechanism; omits deadline extensions, appeal as the real remedy, and the denial-reason and public-reporting duties that began in 2026.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Insider News 08: How to Read an EOB Like a Payer Auditor
summary: Primer on reviewing remittances before posting: compare allowed amounts with the contracted fee schedule, separate contractual write-offs from patient responsibility, watch for repeat shortfalls by procedure code, test bundling denials against NCCI edits, and chase zero-payment lines. Sensible but basic; no news, dates, numbers or sources, one mislabelled code, and it assumes manual EOB reading rather than electronic remittances.
top_ideas: Hold each payer's contracted fee schedule and compare every allowed amount against it at line level before accepting a contractual write-off.
Track shortfalls by payer and procedure code; a repeat on the same code is a systemic underpayment to dispute.
Put zero-payment lines in a review queue instead of letting them post as write-offs.
Check group codes and line balancing before posting so write-offs and patient or secondary balances are never swapped.
red_flags: Labels CO-B15 a bundling flag; it means a required qualifying service was not received or adjudicated, which a distinct-service modifier does not fix.
Check 3 benchmarks allowed against billed charges, which proves nothing; only the contracted or fee-schedule amount is a valid comparator.
Claims payers often issue zero-pay lines with no reason code; electronic remittances must balance with coded adjustments, and no evidence is given.
Offers modifier 59 and X modifiers as a fix with no documentation or audit-risk warning; ignores Qualified Medicare Beneficiary and secondary-payer handling of patient responsibility.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: Insider News 09: Denied Claims Nobody Appealed: The $20K/Month Math Most Practices Ignore
summary: How-to on appealing denials: which categories to pursue or skip, a four-part appeal letter, a weekly 30-minute review, a template library for the top five reason codes and deadline logging on receipt. The headline's $20K-a-month calculation never appears (the text says $2,500), no deadlines or appeal levels are given, and several routes are wrong for Medicare.
top_ideas: Triage denials by expected return into appeal, corrected claim, rebill to the right payer, or prevention only.
Build appeals in four parts: exact denial reason and policy cited, documentation answering each criterion, governing coverage authority, explicit request for reversal and payment.
Log every denial with its appeal deadline on the day it arrives; review new denials on a fixed cycle by reason code with named owners.
Maintain appeal templates and documentation checklists for the highest-volume denial reason codes.
red_flags: Headline promises $20K-a-month math; the text has no calculation and cites only $2,500 a month. Neither figure is sourced.
Tells readers to appeal duplicate denials and resubmit corrected claims; for traditional Medicare, exact duplicates carry no appeal rights and denied claims need reopening or redetermination.
Names the AMA as a specialty society with clinical guidelines and ignores Medicare coverage determinations, the controlling authority for Medicare and Medicare Advantage appeals.
Calls deadline tracking non-negotiable but states no appeal deadline or level; time-saving and success-rate figures are unsourced.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Fits this practice.

title: Insider News 10: Payer Underpayments Are Not Denials. That's Why You're Missing Them.
summary: How-to issue on finding payer underpayments hidden inside contractual write-offs: load contract fee schedules, compare paid claims with contracted rates, sample 25-30 claims monthly, flag variances over $5, separate random from systematic errors and file payment disputes. Contains no news, no sources, and compares payment rather than allowed amount.
top_ideas: Hold every payer's expected allowable in the billing system by code, date, place of service and provider type, and test every remittance line against it automatically.
Separate one-off shortfalls from repeating same-payer, same-code patterns and send each pattern to the payer once, with the affected claims and total dollars.
After each annual rate change, confirm Medicare-linked plans loaded the new rates and read the contract on whether late loading must be corrected retroactively.
Keep a dispute register: governing deadline and its source for each payer, dollars at stake, date filed, outcome and dollars recovered.
red_flags: Compares payment with the contract rate; the valid test is the payer's allowed amount, since payment is net of cost-sharing, sequestration, provider-type and site-of-service differences.
The 3 to 7 percent leakage figure has no source and is referred to as if introduced earlier in the issue; it never is.
Dispute window given as typically 90 to 180 days with no rule cited, and it conflicts with the claim that systematic errors are recoverable back to their start.
No dated news despite the August 2026 date; anesthesia and capitation examples do not fit the stated audience; the working templates sit behind a sales link.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: Insider News 11: PA Denial Appeals: The Step Most Practices Skip Entirely
summary: How-to issue on appealing prior authorization denials: read the denial criterion, assemble a four-part packet (physician letter, chart excerpts, literature, peer-to-peer call), track payer filing windows and follow a seven-step workflow starting with same-day logging. No news, no regulation cited, unsourced win-rate statistics and one arithmetic error.
top_ideas: Log each authorization or coverage denial the day it arrives with the payer's stated reason and a computed appeal deadline.
Keep a one-page rule sheet per payer: appeal window and its source, peer-to-peer availability and window, submission channel, decision deadline.
Try the physician-to-medical-director call first, and write any appeal against the exact criterion quoted in the denial, with chart pages proving each point.
Track appeal outcomes by payer and reason so the overturn rate is the practice's own measured number.
red_flags: Win rates (40-70% on appeal, over 60% on peer-to-peer) have no source and match no public dataset I know of.
Arithmetic error: a 60-day window less four weeks of delay leaves 32 days, not the 16 stated.
Says payers are required to offer peer-to-peer and that contracts set appeal windows; pre-service appeal windows are mainly regulatory and peer-to-peer is not a general legal mandate.
No 2026 content: nothing on the federal prior authorization rule, expedited appeals, good-cause late filing or Medicare Advantage criteria limits; conflates pre-service denials with unpaid claims.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Insider News 12: October 1 Is Days Away. Are Your Codes Ready?
summary: Reminder issue about the fiscal 2027 ICD-10 code update effective October 1, 2026, with four steps and a seven-item checklist: refresh diagnosis lists, confirm vendor update, review the NCD coding transmittal and payer policy changes. Gives no detail of what changed and contains several errors (submission-date rule, CO-4, commercial 'LCDs'). Now past its date.
top_ideas: Keep a code-change calendar with a named owner: diagnosis updates October 1 and April 1, procedure codes and fee schedule January 1.
Before each update, compare every diagnosis code billed in the past year with the official added, deleted and revised list, not only the top 25.
Get written vendor confirmation that the new code set is loaded and applied by date of service; refresh clinician pick-lists and templates.
After each update, watch rejections and denials by reason code as one pattern and correct the source list instead of reworking claims singly.
red_flags: Ties code validity to claim submission date; the rule is date of service or discharge, as Step 3 of the same issue implies.
Mislabels CO-4, which concerns procedure-modifier mismatch; invalid-diagnosis claims are usually rejected up front or returned unprocessable, not denied.
Attributes Local Coverage Determinations to commercial payers and applies hospital terms (charge master, CDI, HIM, ICD-10-PCS) to physician practices.
News issue without the news: no counts or examples of changed codes, no transmittal number; the October 1, 2026 date has already passed.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Insider News 13: Go Get Your Money: The Q4 Revenue Sprint
summary: Year-end checklist with no news: sweep receivables over 90 days by filing limit and dollar value, fix the top three denial codes, bill recent patient balances before the January deductible restart, and check CAQH attestation and Medicare/Medicaid revalidation dates. Basic facts are right, but it confuses filing limits with appeal deadlines and invents a December 31 cutoff.
top_ideas: Scheduled sweep of receivables aged 90+ days that forces each claim into denied, underpaid or never-acknowledged status, ranked by deadline risk first, then dollars.
Chase claims with no remittance: get a payer reference number and resubmit with clearinghouse proof of the original timely submission.
Quarterly ranking of denials by reason and remark code, with a root-cause fix for the top three.
Provider expirables calendar covering CAQH attestation (120 days) and Medicare/Medicaid revalidation, extended to licence, DEA, malpractice and plan recredentialing.
red_flags: Presents December 31 as a hard cutoff for recovering revenue; filing and appeal deadlines actually run from the service or denial date.
Confuses initial filing limits with appeal and corrected-claim deadlines, which govern aged claims already filed; appeal deadlines are never mentioned.
Patient statement push has no carve-out for Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, who cannot be billed Medicare cost-sharing; risky for a dual-eligible population.
Contradictory triage rule (inside filing window first versus dollar value, not date); unsourced 60-90 and 90-120 day credentialing lead times; no author beyond 'Lex'.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Insider News 14: Payers Are Using AI on Your Claims. Is Your Denial Rate Telling You the Truth?
summary: Argues a low denial rate can hide underbilling and unworked write-offs now that payers adjudicate with automation. Recommends reporting initial denial rate, appeal overturn rate and days-to-resolve together, a monthly spike check by payer, reason code and modifier, a recalculated small-denial threshold, and a named human owner for each automated workflow. Its hospital-vendor news is unverified.
top_ideas: Report initial denial rate, appeal overturn rate and days-to-resolve together by payer, adding share of denials appealed and denial write-offs.
Automated spike detection on denials by payer, reason code and modifier, period over period, with a minimum-volume floor and a claim hold on flagged combinations.
Name an owner, an output reviewer and an escalation route for every AI or automated billing workflow.
Reset the small-denial write-off threshold from measured cost-to-work, since agent-run billing makes low-dollar appeals worth pursuing.
red_flags: All news items (Becker's panel, Oracle Health tools, Ensemble and 'Penelope Health', quoted Stanford executive) post-date what I can confirm and are unverified.
Says monthly reports miss automated denial waves, then prescribes monthly reporting and a once-a-month check; '10 minutes' is not credible.
No formulas, denominators, targets or volume floor; scorecard omits appeal rate and denial write-offs, the very problems it warns about.
Treats a high overturn rate as proof of payer error; it can equally reflect the practice's own missing documentation.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Fits this practice.

title: Insider Pulse 01: Three Things Reshaping Independent Practice Revenue Cycles Right Now: ABN Deadline May 2026, Medicaid Coverage Changes and Medicare
summary: Three May 2026 stories: an ABN form renewal with a May 12 switch deadline, Medicaid coverage losses from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and Medicare Advantage plan stress after UnitedHealthcare's 2025 losses. Usable actions are ABN version control, quarterly network checks and 90-day denial trending. The Medicaid story wrongly treats a 2025 law as pending; nothing is sourced.
top_ideas: Quarterly confirmation of in-network status with every Medicare Advantage plan, by product, clinician and location, repeated at each January 1 plan year.
Rolling 90-day trend of Medicare Advantage denials by plan and reason code, flagging codes that previously paid.
Expected-versus-paid comparison against each plan's contract rates to catch out-of-network repricing and underpayments.
Version control for mandated patient notices: log each ABN template's printed expiration date and every location where a copy lives.
red_flags: Calls the One Big Beautiful Bill Act pending in May 2026; to my knowledge it became law July 4, 2025. No enacted effective dates are given.
'11.8 to 17 million losing Medicaid' appears to relabel estimates of total uninsured increases as Medicaid losses; attributed to CBO without citation.
Unsourced '40 to 60 percent' out-of-network gap conflicts with the rule that Medicare Advantage plans pay non-contracted providers Original Medicare amounts for covered services.
ABN dates (March 13, May 12, 2026) unverified and consequences overstated; deadline passed six months ago; UnitedHealthcare facts are stale 2025 items.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Insider Pulse 02: (June 2026): CMS Just Handed Your Chronic Care Patients to a Tech Platform. Here's What Happens Next.
summary: June 2026 three-story brief: the CMS ACCESS model starting July 5, 2026 and its possible pull on chronic care management revenue; Medicare Advantage 2027 filings as a predictor of plan exits; and electronic prior authorization. Watch-list advice only, no sources. The ACCESS participant description and the prior-authorization legal basis look wrong.
top_ideas: Keep a current roster of CCM-enrolled patients and trend monthly billed CCM volume, so engagement lost to outside programs shows up within a month or two.
Trend trailing-90-day denial rate separately for each Medicare Advantage payer as an early signal of a plan tightening before exits or benefit cuts are announced.
Verify network participation with every MA plan quarterly and keep a written contingency plan for each payer's exit, sized by its share of charges.
Schedule payer reviews on the yearly Medicare Advantage cycle: June filings, fall plan landscape, October Star Ratings, year-end enrollment.
red_flags: Credits an unenacted bill (Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act) for the January 1, 2026 rule; timeframes come from CMS-0057-F, whose electronic API deadline is January 1, 2027. Verify.
Says ACCESS participants are not physician groups; Part B-enrolled practices appear eligible, and the issue omits the co-management payment for primary care clinicians. Verify.
Claims Star Ratings will report prior-authorization compliance from 2027 and that plans under 3.5 stars face penalties; no such measure known, and the bonus cut-off is 4 stars.
No author, citation or link; hyperbole ('UnitedHealthcare financial collapse', CMS 'handed' patients to tech platforms); no formulas, thresholds, payment amounts or templates.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Insider Pulse 03: (July 2026): The Compliance Deadline Passed. The Problem Didn't.
summary: July 2026 brief: repeats the electronic prior-authorization story, argues Medicaid unwinding left uncollectable patient balances to review for write-off, and lists audit triggers with a three-step self-check. Useful residue is an aged-AR cleanup plus E/M distribution and chart audits; the legal basis, dates, thresholds and audit claims are unreliable and unsourced.
top_ideas: Benchmark each provider's trailing-12-month E/M level distribution against Medicare specialty peer data, using the code families the practice actually bills.
Run a recurring random chart sample per provider testing whether documented problems, data and risk support the billed level; fix templates and handle any overpayments found.
Review aged Medicaid and self-pay balances against coverage dates once, checking retroactive eligibility before write-off, and classify write-offs correctly under a written policy.
Re-verify coverage on a fixed recurring schedule for ongoing patients, and keep timestamped payer portal records as evidence for appeals.
red_flags: Lead story repeats the wrong legal basis (an unenacted bill) for a January 1, 2026 electronic prior-authorization mandate, adds a real-time decision duty not in force, and cites no data.
Dates the MDM shift for 99214/99215 to 2023; office-visit rules changed in 2021. The 15-20-point 99215 threshold is unsourced and far too loose to detect an outlier.

Calls post-disenrollment Medicaid balances almost certainly uncollectable, ignoring retroactive eligibility, reinstatements and dual-eligible protections; silent on the 2025 law's Medicaid redetermination changes.
Claims commercial payers audit practices whose Medicaid share fell, which a single payer cannot observe; 'audits rose measurably' has no figure or source.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.

title: Insider Pulse 04: Q4 Is Coming. The Practices That Prepare in August Win in November.
summary: August 2026 issue with no actual news: three seasonal essays urging August rate-renegotiation requests for January 1, quarterly write-off review with a 20-claim underpayment test, and early eligibility, deductible and Medicare plan-landscape checks before year-end. Unsourced; premises such as contracts renewing January 1 are wrong, and figures like 5-10% rate gains look invented.
top_ideas: Compare the allowed amount on every remittance line with the expected contract amount, net of legitimate reductions, instead of the issue's 20-claim sample; send variances to a dispute queue.
Review write-offs and adjustments by reason code quarterly or monthly; treat every timely-filing write-off as a defect traced from service date to first submission.
Keep a contract register with each agreement's true renewal date, notice periods and rates as a percent of Medicare for the 20 highest-revenue codes.
Each autumn read the CMS landscape files for the service-area counties, then re-verify eligibility for the whole census in early January and monthly for facility residents.
red_flags: No news at all: no rule, agency action or payer event is reported; three evergreen essays with manufactured August urgency and zero citations.
Says payer contracts renew January 1 and need 90-180 days' modification notice; provider agreements usually renew on their own anniversary dates and notice terms are contract-specific.
Unsupported numbers: 5-10% rate gains, two to three hours of preparation, 85% versus 60% patient collections, a 20% trigger on a 20-claim sample.

Deductible logic is backwards; 'open enrollment October through December' blurs Medicare's October 15-December 7 period; CMS landscape files have recently been released in late September, not October.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Insider Pulse 05: Your Q4 Credentialing Window Is Closing
summary: September 2026 issue, again without news: a credentialing piece framed as a closing 'Q4 window'. It covers new-hire payer enrollment, location changes, CAQH re-attestation, licence and DEA expirations, group-versus-individual enrollment mismatch and a four-step checklist ending in a master calendar. Useful hygiene, but the Medicare Advantage 'October deadline' looks invented, traditional Medicare is ignored and the date arithmetic fails.
top_ideas: Keep one master credentialing calendar per clinician covering licences, DEA, certification, CAQH attestation, Medicare revalidation and payer enrollment status, reviewed monthly by a named owner.
Confirm in writing with every payer that each clinician is linked to the group's tax ID and NPI, and that Medicare reassignment is on file.
Start payer enrollment at offer acceptance; track submission date, confirmation number and status by payer; escalate to the enrollment unit after three weeks of silence.
Re-attest CAQH ahead of the 120-day cycle with 30- and 15-day alerts, and reconcile addresses across NPPES, PECOS, CAQH, payers and the billing system.
red_flags: Central premise looks invented: no general 'October enrollment deadline' locks clinicians out of Medicare Advantage networks; credentialing is rolling and not tied to quarters.
Date arithmetic fails: 90 days from July 15 is mid-October, not before October 1; an October 1 application at 60-90 days does finish within the fourth quarter.
Overstates CAQH: a lapsed attestation stalls credentialing, but 'automatic suspension' of participating clinicians is not a rule I recognise; the portal name used is outdated.

Never mentions traditional Medicare enrollment (filing-date effective date, 30-day retroactive billing, 30-day location reporting), so 'revenue not recoverable' is wrong for a Medicare fee-for-service practice.
verdict: Unreliable on rules and numbers. Use only as a list of topics.

title: Insider Pulse 06: (October 2026): The Denial Code That's Quietly Draining Your AR
summary: October 2026 issue explaining three remittance adjustment codes (CO-4 modifiers, CO-16 missing data, CO-97 bundling), reporting the October 1 quarterly Medicare correct-coding edit update (Version 32.3), and giving a five-step loop: log denials by reason and remark code, assign owners, fix claim then rule, send MA130 claims to correction, review weekly. One real news item; the rest is evergreen.
top_ideas: Log every denial by reason code plus remark code (adding payer, CPT and dollars) and review the top three combinations weekly for 15 minutes.
Hard-code the Medicare rule: claims returned unprocessable with remark code MA130 are corrected and resubmitted as new claims, never sent to redetermination.
Fix each recurring denial twice: on the claim, then in the charge rule, scrubber edit or agent instruction that produced it, with a named owner.
After every quarterly edit update (next: January 1, 2027), confirm the scrubber's edit version and compare denial patterns before and after.
red_flags: Ties correct-coding edit denials only to CO-97 and CO-4; Medicare contractors generally use reason code 236 (151 for unit edits), never mentioned. Verify on First Coast remittances.
Says unsupported modifier 59 use is where CO-4 comes from; code 4 is a code-modifier validity edit, and unsupported overrides usually pay, then surface in audits.
Only one dated news item, and its action window (first two weeks of October 2026) has passed; Version 32.3 and Change Request 14516 are unverified.
Headline promises one AR-draining code and delivers none; Experian's 90% human-review figure is unconfirmed; no source links; the denial log is described, not supplied.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting.

title: Insider Pulse 07: (November 2026): Prior Auth Is Shrinking on Paper. Here's What Actually Changes for Your Claims.
summary: November 2026 prior authorization news brief: UnitedHealthcare dropped about 1,700 codes October 1 (about 120 in Medicare Advantage); federal rule duties live since January 2026 with a payer API due January 1, 2027; a West Virginia law and a Texas investigation. Advises reconciling payer lists to own codes, logging turnaround by plan, and questioning the EHR vendor.
top_ideas: Split every payer announcement by plan type and match it to your own codes before changing workflow; only about 120 removed codes touch Medicare Advantage.
Keep a dated request log by plan with alerts at 72 hours (urgent) and seven days (standard) for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care.
Maintain a payer rule matrix refreshed monthly; when an authorization requirement is removed, re-check documentation against medical policy because review moves to after the service.
Ask system vendors in writing what will be live on January 1, 2027, for which payers, with what fallback; watch for CMS enforcement discretion.
red_flags: Post-June-2026 events (UnitedHealthcare's 1,700 codes, AMA letter, Texas investigation) rest on trade-press bylines without links; none can be confirmed from my own knowledge.
KFF figures (12% Medicare Advantage denials, two-thirds overturned) differ from KFF's earlier analyses (about 6-8% and 80%); KFF is absent from the sources line.
Treats 2026 rule duties as uniform from January 1; omits that drugs are excluded, managed-care dates vary and extensions exist; names no complaint channel for the promised leverage.
Silently reverses Issues 02-03, which blamed a January 2026 electronic deadline on a different statute; gold card described as covering most procedures, likely overstated.
verdict: A usable outline. Check every rule and number before acting. Little of it fits a facility-based practice.
